Independent benchmark · October 2026 · open source on GitHub

Sarvam Field Test

Sarvam AI's speech, translation, document and chat models against Google Gemini, OpenAI, Anthropic Claude and self-hosted open weights, on twelve jobs Indian businesses actually do. Every test has known answers, so scoring is automatic and no model grades another.

The short answer

What to use for which job

Sarvam is the specialist pick for Indian speech and for translating into Indian languages. For reasoning over text, documents and code, a price-matched Gemini, OpenAI or Claude model was more accurate in every test.

Speech recognition, Indian languages
Saaras v3. Lowest word error rate in 12 of 13 languages and about 4× faster than Gemini. For calls where amounts and account digits matter, Gemini 3.8 Flash captured them exactly 94% of the time against Saaras's 81%, because Saaras often spells numbers out as words.
Real-time voice bot
All-Sarvam stack (Saaras → Sarvam-105B → Bulbul): first audio in about 1.5 s, replies in the caller's language 19 of 20 times, ₹1.56 per conversation-minute. The all-Gemini stack read numbers back more accurately but took about 6.8 s.
Text-to-speech
Bulbul v3. As intelligible as Gemini and OpenAI voices across 10 languages, with the fastest first audio.
Translating into Indian languages
Sarvam-Translate (best in 8 of 10 languages). Avoid Mayura for anything with numbers. Translating into English: Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Haiku or GPT-5.4 mini, all well ahead of Sarvam.
KYC, invoices, land records
Gemini 3.8 Flash or Claude Sonnet 5.5 on the image. Clean scans are a tie at about 99.5% for everyone; on bad phone photos Sarvam Vision invented fluent text that was not on the page, and OpenAI models misread Indian-script names.
Chat, Q&A, business text
Gemini 3.8 Flash or GPT-5.4 mini. Sarvam-105B gets close only with thinking on, which costs 5–20 s per answer and sometimes returns nothing.
Clinical notes
Gemini 3.8 Flash, on the text or straight on the audio. No cloud model invented a medicine in 40 consultations.
Coding agents
Gemini 3.8 Flash passed all 160 task-language items first try, Claude Haiku 5.5 99% and GPT-5.4 mini 92–98%. Sarvam-105B passed 56–69%, and none of the Aadhaar-checksum tasks.
Data must stay on your servers
Qwen3-30B over Sarvam-30B for accuracy (84% vs 63% on business tasks). Sarvam-30B is faster per token and much cheaper to feed Indian text, but ignores format instructions. Neither refuses out-of-scope questions without thinking on.

What cuts across the twelve tests

Five patterns

1. Sarvam-105B's thinking mode is a gamble

With thinking off (reasoning_effort: null) Sarvam-105B answers in about 0.5–1.5 s. With thinking on it is more accurate on structured tasks, but answers take 5–46 s and the reasoning length is unpredictable: 29% of coding calls and 16 of 80 legal summaries came back empty because reasoning used the whole token budget, and you still pay for those tokens. Setting "low" did not reduce thinking. Leave at least 16k output tokens of headroom if you turn it on.

2. Self-hosted Sarvam-30B knows the facts but not the format

Sarvam removed Sarvam-30B from its API, so self-hosting the open weights is the only way to use it. On this Mac it ran faster than Qwen3-30B (about 27 vs 19 tokens/s) and needed less memory, but it labelled Tamil, Telugu and Bengali tickets as "Hinglish", wrote CRM notes in the wrong language, appended unrequested explanations, and invented answers to out-of-scope questions. Its thinking cannot be switched off through the chat API; only pre-filling an empty <think></think> works.

3. Sarvam's tokenizer is the cheapest way to send Indian text

The same sentence costs 1.55× its English token count on Sarvam's tokenizer, 1.89× on Gemini's, 2.10× on OpenAI's, 3.44× on Claude's and 5.89× on Qwen3's. Sarvam's vocabulary is Gemma's with about 22,800 slots re-assigned to Indian scripts, so the saving is largest on Odia, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Gujarati and Punjabi.

4. Under stress, models invent rather than leave blanks

On badly photographed documents Sarvam Vision wrote fluent text that was not on the page, and GPT-5.5 invented firm names and GST numbers. Sarvam-105B without thinking added deadline dates and totals it had computed itself to 9% of legal summaries. Every cloud model refused all ten out-of-scope farming questions; both self-hosted models invented answers such as 150 kg of DAP per acre for a crop the sheet never covered.

5. Answering in the user's language is still unsolved

Asked in English about a Hindi or Tamil document, most models answered in the document's script: GPT-5.4 mini replied in English 7% of the time and Sarvam-105B 11%. Romanised questions (Hinglish, Tanglish) got a romanised reply from no price-matched model more than 69% of the time. Only the frontier models matched the user every time.

Method

How it was run

Six parallel agents built and ran the twelve suites on one Apple M5 Max (128 GB) between 19:30 and 23:30 IST on 11 October 2026, sharing one Python library for API clients, scoring and result files. Systems were called through their official APIs; Claude through OpenRouter; Sarvam-30B and Qwen3-30B through llama.cpp on the same Mac.

  • Known answers only. Every item has a gold answer (a number, code, label, fact list or reference text) and is scored by code. No model judges another's free text. Where speech or translation quality needed a reference, public datasets (FLEURS/FLORES, CC-BY 4.0) or round-trip transcription by two or three different vendors' transcribers were used.
  • Mostly synthetic, realistic data. Invoices, KYC forms, WhatsApp orders, policies, consultations and legal passages were written for this benchmark, with fake people and clearly marked sample IDs. None were reviewed by native speakers; treat absolute scores as indicative and the comparisons as the result.
  • Same inputs, both modes. Sarvam-105B ran with thinking off and on; Gemini Flash with thinking off (and on where it mattered). Frontier models (Gemini Pro, GPT-5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5) ran on fixed 30-item subsets to show the ceiling.
  • Uncertainty shown. 95% bootstrap confidence intervals on every score; hover any bar for its interval and sample size.
  • Sandboxed code. Model-written code ran only inside a macOS sandbox with no network, no reads of the home folder and no writes outside a temporary folder.
  • Resumable and auditable. Every model output is kept in results/raw/*.jsonl; reruns only call the API for missing items.

Use case 1Sarvam behind

Code-mixed voice support & collections calls

A bank, telecom or insurer handling Hinglish/Tanglish/Manglish/Benglish/Kanglish calls: which speech-to-text gets the caller's card digits, amounts, dates and phone numbers right, and which voice-agent stack answers fastest?

uc01 code-mixed customer-care utterances · n=80 · synthetic, written for this benchmark · licence: CC-BY-4.0 (this repo)

Verdict

For capturing what a collections or card-services call actually needs — the digits — use gemini-3.8-flash as the transcriber or add a number-normalisation step after saaras: Gemini got 94% of amounts, card digits, dates and phone numbers exactly, saaras:v3 codemix 74-81%, gpt-4o-transcribe ~60%, hosted whisper-1 ~50%. Use saaras:v3 codemix (not transcribe) when latency matters: it returns in ~0.6 s versus 1.2 s (gpt-4o-transcribe) and 3.9 s (Gemini), and has the lowest CER on phone-line audio. For the full voice loop, Sarvam's speech ends (saaras + bulbul, ~0.9 s combined) are the fastest available; sarvam-105b is the fastest reply LLM at p50 and the most reliable at answering in the caller's language, while gpt-5.4-mini gives steadier tail latency but often switches Dravidian/Bengali callers to Hindi or English. The all-Gemini stack is the most accurate on numbers but takes ~6.8 s to start speaking. Do not use Whisper (local or hosted) for code-mixed Indian calls.

Findings

  • Entity accuracy (what a bank needs: card last-4, amounts, dates, phone and claim numbers, 100 entities): gemini-3.8-flash 0.94 [0.89-0.98] on both clean and phone-line audio; saaras:v3 codemix 0.74 [0.65-0.83] clean / 0.81 [0.73-0.88] phone; gpt-4o-transcribe 0.61 / 0.57; whisper-1 (hosted Whisper) 0.50 / 0.51; saaras:v3 transcribe 0.43 / 0.46; local whisper-large-v3-turbo 0.24 / 0.26.
  • Most saaras misses are formatting, not hearing: in codemix mode 15 of 26 clean misses (11 of 19 phone) had no digits at all — the number came back as words (e.g. hi02 'बारह हज़ार चार सौ निन्यानवे', 'सेवन थ्री ज़ीरो सिक्स'). Codemix mode is not applied consistently: 48/160 codemix outputs contain no Latin letters at all, i.e. it fell back to transcribe-style output. Transcribe mode writes numbers as words almost always (51 of 57 misses). Add inverse text normalisation before using saaras output for account data.
  • Gemini never wrote a number as words (0 such misses); its 6 misses were genuinely wrong digits. It does not follow the script convention reliably either: 59/160 Gemini outputs had no Latin letters (English loanwords written in native script).
  • Word error rate is convention-bound. Against the code-mix reference, saaras codemix and Gemini tie on clean audio (0.38 vs 0.36) and saaras codemix is better on phone audio (0.30 [0.24-0.36] vs 0.35 [0.31-0.39]); CER on phone audio 0.24 vs 0.37. Scoring each output against whichever reference convention suits it better (code-mix or all-native script, no transliteration), Gemini is lower: 0.17-0.18 vs saaras codemix 0.25.
  • Phone-line degradation (8 kHz, 300-3400 Hz, mu-law, 20 dB SNR) barely hurt any API system; saaras codemix even scored better on phone than clean, which reflects run-to-run variation in its number formatting rather than a real benefit.
  • Whisper is not usable for code-mixed Indian calls. Local whisper-large-v3-turbo: WER 0.80 (per-clip capped at 1), entity accuracy 0.24, repetition loops on noisy audio, Malayalam answered in Devanagari on 15 of 32 clips even with language='ml'. Hosted whisper-1 is somewhat better (WER 0.72, entities 0.50) but rejects language='bn' and 'ml' outright (HTTP 400 'Language 'bn' is not supported.'), so Benglish and Manglish ran on auto-detect.
  • gpt-4o-transcribe (given the same code-mix instruction as Gemini via its prompt field) lands between saaras and Whisper: WER 0.60 / 0.58, best-of-two-references WER 0.35, entity accuracy 0.61 / 0.57. It is strongly voice-sensitive: entity accuracy 0.76 on Gemini-voiced clips but 0.35 on macOS `say` clips, where it often wrote numbers as words ('आठ हजार सात सौ पचास') or dropped digits (reference 417209 -> 47209). Fastest non-Sarvam STT: p50 1.17 s.
  • Latency per 5-15 s utterance: saaras:v3 p50 0.61 s / p95 0.95 s (RTF ~0.10); gpt-4o-transcribe 1.17 / 1.46 s (RTF 0.19); whisper-1 2.34 / 3.71 s; gemini-3.8-flash 3.9 / 6.8 s (RTF 0.67); local Whisper on a shared, loaded GPU p50 7.9 s.
  • Voice-agent pipeline (20 turns; time to first audio = STT + full LLM reply + TTS first byte), p50 / p95: Sarvam stack (saaras codemix + sarvam-105b think off + bulbul:v3 stream) 1.48 / 20.5 s; saaras + gpt-5.4-mini + bulbul 2.01 / 2.27 s; OpenAI stack (gpt-4o-transcribe + gpt-5.4-mini + gpt-4o-mini-tts stream) 3.17 / 3.70 s; saaras + claude-haiku-5.5 + bulbul 3.31 / 4.42 s; Gemini stack (gemini STT + gemini-3.8-flash + gemini TTS stream) 6.78 / 23.1 s. LLM p50: sarvam-105b 0.46 s, gpt-5.4-mini 1.12-1.18 s, claude-haiku-5.5 2.40 s, gemini-3.8-flash 2.40 s. TTS first byte p50: bulbul 0.35-0.39 s, gpt-4o-mini-tts 0.81 s, gemini TTS 1.13 s. sarvam-105b's p95 is driven by one 19.5 s reply on a shared account; gpt-5.4-mini was the most consistent.
  • Agent quality, reply in the caller's language and script (>=30% of letters in the caller's script): sarvam-105b 19/20, claude-haiku-5.5 18/20, gemini-3.8-flash 16/20, gpt-5.4-mini 12/20 (OpenAI stack) and 11/20 (on saaras transcripts). gpt-5.4-mini answered Malayalam, Bengali and Kannada callers in Hindi or English 4 times (e.g. 'Sorry for the परेशानी… Aapka ₹560 debit ho gaya' to a Malayalam caller); claude-haiku-5.5 did so once; sarvam-105b never (its one miss was English to a Malayalam caller). Numbers read back correctly: Gemini stack 29/30, Sarvam stack 25/30, OpenAI stack 25/30, saaras+haiku 24/30, saaras+gpt-5.4-mini 23/30 — misheard STT digits propagate ('UPI' -> 'UP', 915 -> 945). claude-haiku-5.5 was the wordiest (~3.9k output tokens over 20 turns vs ~0.7-1.2k for the others), which lengthens TTS.
  • gemini-3.8-flash with thinking_budget=0 still spent 419-630 thinking tokens on 3 of 20 agent turns (and ~290 on others in a discarded first run, where a 300-token cap truncated replies mid-sentence); the final run used a 1000-token cap. 'Think off' is not a hard switch on this model.
  • Cost per conversation-minute (caller + agent audio), all-Sarvam stack at list prices: saaras STT Rs 0.23 + sarvam-105b Rs 0.015 + bulbul TTS Rs 1.32 (441 chars/min at Rs 30 per 10k chars) = Rs 1.56; TTS is 85% of it. Swapping the LLM for gpt-5.4-mini or claude-haiku-5.5 raises bulbul's share because those replies are longer (Rs 1.52 and Rs 1.81 per minute for TTS alone); claude-haiku-5.5 via OpenRouter cost USD 0.0022 for all 20 turns as reported. Gemini and OpenAI usage is recorded per conversation-minute in agent_pipeline (tokens/characters; not priced here).
  • Sarvam API behaviour under a shared account (other agents active): one window returned HTTP 402 'No credits available' for every call, and STT/TTS/LLM calls hit 429 'Rate limit exceeded'. 87 STT calls ended as HTTP 400 'Failed to read the file' — these were our harness's fault, not Sarvam's: common/bench.py sarvam_post retries a 429 by re-sending the same, already-read file handle, i.e. an empty upload. Re-opening the file per attempt fixed it. Production clients need backoff on 429 and must rebuild multipart bodies on retry.

Caveats

  • Audio is synthetic (macOS `say` Indian voices for Hindi/Tamil/Bengali/Kannada, gemini-3.8-flash-tts for the rest and all Malayalam). TTS speech is cleaner and more regular than real callers; absolute error rates on real calls will be higher.
  • Possible home advantage for Gemini on Gemini-voiced audio: on the 64 non-Malayalam clips per source, Gemini entity accuracy is 0.92 on `say` audio vs 0.97 on Gemini audio, but saaras codemix also improves (0.68 -> 0.81), so Gemini's lead holds on audio it did not generate.
  • Gemini TTS read a style instruction aloud in 38 of 48 clips in the first synthesis pass; those clips were regenerated from the bare text and every STT result on them re-run. No clip was hand-checked by listening.
  • References were written by one author; spellings of English loanwords in native script vary (யுபிஐ/யூபிஐ), which inflates every system's WER. That is why entity accuracy, not WER, is the headline.
  • Entity matching joins digit groups and ignores separators but does not convert number words to digits. A deployment with an inverse-text-normalisation step would recover many saaras misses; the score measures raw API output.
  • 80 utterances, 100 entities per condition: CIs are roughly +/-0.05 to +/-0.09. Per-language numbers rest on 16 utterances each and are indicative only.
  • Agent latency was measured from a Mac in India over the public internet on one afternoon, on a shared Sarvam account under load from other jobs; LLM replies were not streamed (full response time), TTS was streamed (time to first byte).

Use case 2Level

Citizen helpline speech-to-text across India's languages

A state or national citizen helpline takes calls in many Indian languages: which speech-to-text works in all of them, and how bad is its weakest language?

FLEURS (google/fleurs) test split · n=350 · public data · licence: CC-BY-4.0

Verdict

For a multi-language citizen helpline, saaras:v3 is the strongest default: lowest WER in 12 of the 13 comparable languages (several near-ties), macro CER about half of Gemini's and gpt-4o-transcribe's, every clip transcribed, and answers in under a second. Plan for its two gaps: it writes Sindhi only in Devanagari, and it accepts at most 30 s per REST call. Gemini-3.8-flash (worst language Assamese 0.31) and gpt-4o-transcribe (worst Nepali 0.42, never blocks, 1.4 s) are the credible alternatives and both handle Arabic-script Sindhi; Gemini silently returned nothing for about 3% of clips. Whisper — hosted whisper-1 or local large-v3-turbo — is not fit for an Indian helpline: it rejects or mis-scripts six of the fourteen languages.

Findings

  • In the 13 languages where its output script matches FLEURS, saaras:v3 has the lowest WER in 12 (all except Urdu; Nepali 0.271 vs 0.272 and Telugu 0.170 vs 0.173 are ties; on CER Gemini wins Telugu, Marathi and Urdu): macro WER 0.17 / CER 0.052 vs gemini-3.8-flash 0.21 / 0.090, gpt-4o-transcribe 0.27 / 0.090, whisper-1 (hosted) 0.79 / 0.54 and whisper-large-v3-turbo (local) 0.75 / 0.45. Biggest saaras leads: Assamese 0.16 vs 0.31, Malayalam 0.17 vs 0.27, Punjabi 0.15 vs 0.23 (Gemini figures include its blocked clips).
  • Worst language: saaras Nepali 0.27 [0.22-0.33], Gemini Assamese 0.31 [0.21-0.42], Whisper Malayalam 1.00. Gemini's worst-language CI overlaps saaras's, so on read speech the two are close on the weakest language; Whisper is not.
  • gpt-4o-transcribe is the most robust OpenAI option and the only system besides Gemini that writes every language, including Sindhi, in the reference script: WER worst language Nepali 0.42 [0.32-0.53], best CER of all systems on Tamil (0.091), zero blocked clips, p50 1.4 s (RTF 0.12). Its WER trails saaras in 12 of 13 comparable languages (it wins only Urdu, and on CER also Tamil); the gap is mostly word boundaries and spelling choices — its macro CER (0.090) equals Gemini's.
  • Sindhi: saaras:v3 (language_code sd-IN) writes Sindhi in Devanagari, FLEURS uses Perso-Arabic script, so it scores WER 0.996 here. The Devanagari text reads as a faithful transcript (e.g. 'होस्टाइल माहौल वारे कोर्स…' for 'هوسٽائل ماحول واري ڪورس…'), so this is a script choice, not deafness — but a helpline that needs Arabic-script Sindhi cannot get it from saaras. Gemini handles Sindhi in Arabic script at WER 0.21.
  • Gemini returned no transcript at all for 20 of 350 clips on the first try (prompt blocked, block_reason OTHER) and for 11 (3.1%) even after three attempts, spread over 7 languages (Assamese 3, Punjabi 2, Malayalam 2, Bengali, Tamil, Kannada, Odia 1 each). On the clips it did transcribe, its macro WER is 0.185. A helpline using Gemini needs a fallback for blocked audio.
  • Hosted whisper-1 rejects language codes bn, te, gu, pa ('Language 'bn' is not supported.', HTTP 400) and has no Odia, so those ran on auto-detect; it then wrote Bengali, Gujarati, Malayalam, Odia, Punjabi and Sindhi mostly in the wrong script, and Assamese/Telugu at CER >= 0.5. Only Hindi (0.30) and Urdu (0.24) are usable — no better than the local model.
  • Whisper-large-v3-turbo cannot serve five of the fourteen languages: with the language forced it still wrote Punjabi in Devanagari (23/25), Assamese in Devanagari (18/25), Malayalam in Devanagari or Kannada script (23/25), and Sindhi mostly in Devanagari; it has no Odia at all and auto-detect wrote Odia audio in Gujarati script (20/25). Only Urdu (0.21) and Hindi (0.28) are usable.
  • Speed per clip (5-30 s of audio): saaras p50 0.87 s / p95 2.3 s (RTF 0.09); gpt-4o-transcribe 1.4 / 2.2 s (RTF 0.12); whisper-1 3.0 / 6.6 s (RTF 0.28); Gemini 3.9 / 7.0 s (RTF 0.36); local Whisper p50 8.6 s (RTF 0.84) on a GPU shared with a 30B llama.cpp server.
  • saaras:v3 REST rejects clips over 30 s ('use the batch API'), so long callers must be chunked or sent through the job API. 74 calls first ended as HTTP 400 'Failed to read the file'; these followed 429 rate-limit retries in common/bench.py, which re-sends an already-read file handle (an empty upload), and all succeeded when the file was re-opened per attempt.
  • Cost: 350 clips (72.6 min) cost Rs 36.3 on saaras at the Rs 30/hour list price; Gemini used 116k input / 16k output tokens, gpt-4o-transcribe 47k input / 20k output tokens, whisper-1 72.6 billed minutes for the same audio.

Caveats

  • FLEURS is read Wikipedia sentences recorded by volunteers on decent microphones: easier than real helpline calls (spontaneous speech, code-mixing, 8 kHz phone lines, background noise). Expect higher error rates in production, and see uc01 for phone-line and code-mixed results.
  • 25 clips per language (first 25 distinct sentences <= 30 s in archive order); per-language CIs are wide (often +/-0.05 to +/-0.10 WER). Rankings between saaras and Gemini inside one language are often not significant; the macro averages and Whisper's failures are.
  • Urdu is FLEURS ur_pk (Pakistani speakers) and Nepali is ne_np; Indian Urdu/Nepali speakers may differ.
  • WER on Indic text is harsh: agglutinative words, optional nukta/halant spellings and number formatting all count as errors. CER is the fairer cross-language number; both are reported.
  • Sindhi is scored against Perso-Arabic references only; nothing is transliterated, so saaras's Devanagari Sindhi is counted as wrong. The 'excluding other-script languages' worst-language metric shows the result without it.
  • Gemini's blocked clips count as WER 1.0. FLEURS sentences come from Wikipedia, so the block may be a recitation/content filter that real calls would trigger less often — unverified.
  • Whisper latency was measured on a shared Mac whose GPU was also serving other benchmark jobs.

Use case 3Level

Documents: KYC, GST invoices, land records and bills in Indian scripts

Can I digitise Indian-language business documents (GST invoices, KYC forms, land records, utility bills, ration cards) into correct structured fields, from clean scans and from phone photos, and which stack should I use?

uc03-synthetic-indic-docs · n=60 · synthetic, written for this benchmark · licence: CC0 (synthetic); fonts are macOS system fonts used only to render images

Verdict

For clean scans and ordinary phone photos of Indian-script business documents, any of these stacks reads about 99.5% of fields correctly. Choose on cost, latency and where the data may go. The all-Sarvam pipeline (Vision plus sarvam-105b) costs about ₹0.52 per page and runs on an Indian provider. Gemini on the image is faster at p95 (8.7 s vs 33.5 s) and simpler, since it needs no job API. Poor photos are the exception. There, Gemini on the image was clearly more robust (93% of fields and 56% of pages fully right, against 86% and 25%), and Sarvam Vision sometimes wrote fluent text that was not on the page, occasionally in the wrong script. So if your intake is mostly phone photos taken by customers or field staff, use Gemini, or put an image-quality gate and a re-capture step in front of Sarvam Vision. With either stack, validate IDs such as PAN and GSTIN by format and checksum. Among the added comparators, claude-sonnet-5.5 was the most accurate on bad photos, and claude-haiku-5.5 matched the leaders on clean and normal photos at about $0.37 per 1,000 pages. OpenAI's gpt-5.4-mini and gpt-5.5 misread or invented Indic-script values far more often in this test, so don't use them for this job without validation.

Findings

  • Clean scans and ordinary phone photos are essentially solved by all three stacks. Field exact-match: clean 99.5% (Sarvam Vision + sarvam-105b), 99.5% (Sarvam Vision + Gemini), 99.6% (Gemini on the image). Phone photo: 99.3% / 99.5% / 99.3%. The CIs overlap completely (60 pages, 783 fields each). Pages with every field correct: 93-95% clean, 92-93% photo.
  • Bad photos separate the stacks. On the 16-page harsh subset (6 deg tilt, strong skew, hand shadow, noise, 0.55x resolution, JPEG q 22-30), Gemini on the image kept 92.8% of fields [87.2, 97.2] and got 56% of pages fully right. The Sarvam pipeline kept 85.6% [78.5, 92.1] and 25% of pages. Swapping sarvam-105b for Gemini as the extractor on the same Vision text only moved this to 86.5%, so the gap is OCR, not extraction.
  • Text accuracy tells the same story. Order-free CER for Sarvam Vision vs Gemini OCR is 0.020 vs 0.023 clean and 0.015 vs 0.004 photo, then 0.193 vs 0.028 on harsh photos (gold-word recall 0.84 vs 0.95). The harsh-photo CER by script for Vision is worst in Tamil (0.32), Bengali (0.21) and Devanagari (0.20).
  • On degraded pages Sarvam Vision writes fluent text that is not on the page. The Tamil patta header 'மாதிரி ஆவணம்' (sample document) came out as 'எதிரி ஆயுதம் - தற்காப்பு' (enemy weapon - defence). A line of Kannada about Belagavi district appeared inside the Tamil page. The 7/12 subtitle '(पिकांची नोंदवही)' became '(पिंपरी चिंचवड)', a real Pune place name, and sarvam-105b then put that into the taluka field. During the smoke test, a Kannada line on a mixed-script page also came back in Bengali script.
  • Handwriting-style PANs expose character confusions. Sarvam Vision misread I/1 and O/0 in 3 of 10 KYC forms (e.g. FADPQ1032L read as FADPQI032L, HLOPM1790W as HLOPM179OW), the same way on clean and photo pages. Gemini got 1 of 10 wrong. A PAN or GSTIN format and checksum check would catch these, whichever OCR you use.
  • Latency per page, p50 / p95: Sarvam Vision job 5.9 s / 25.3 s (the job API queues; one job per page), Vision + sarvam-105b 9.2 s / 33.5 s, Gemini on the image 5.0 s / 8.7 s.
  • Cost per 1,000 pages: the Sarvam pipeline is ₹521 (Vision ₹500 at ₹0.50/page, plus ₹20.9 of sarvam-105b tokens). Gemini on the image uses about 1.30M input and 0.19M output tokens per 1,000 pages; multiply by your Gemini rate. Running Vision + Gemini costs Vision's ₹500 plus about 0.62M/0.19M Gemini tokens.
  • Sarvam Vision API quirks. Insufficient credits return HTTP 400 'Insufficient credits for 1 pages' from /start, not 402 as on chat. Uploads must be a PDF or a ZIP, so a single photo has to be zipped. The status payload names the input 'document.pdf' even for a ZIP. Output is a ZIP holding document.md (tables as HTML <table>/<br/>, not pipe markdown) plus metadata/page_NNN.json with block coordinates and reading order. The job needs a language code, so a mixed-language intake also needs language detection first.
  • Price-matched cloud tier on the image, field accuracy clean / photo / harsh: claude-haiku-5.5 (via OpenRouter) scored 99.7% / 98.8% / 76.4%. openai:gpt-5.4-mini scored 89.1% / 83.3% / 56.1%, with only 30% of clean pages fully correct. Its errors are genuine misreads of Indic names and numbers; on clean pages it got patta owner names wrong on 10 of 10. Latency p50: gpt-5.4-mini 1.4 s, haiku 2.9 s. Cost: haiku about $0.37 per 1,000 pages (OpenRouter usage.cost); gpt-5.4-mini uses about 2.3M input tokens per 1,000 pages.
  • Frontier ceiling, think on, on the fixed 30 images (16 harsh plus 14 phone photos), field accuracy: - claude-sonnet-5.5: 96.4% [93.4, 98.7], 77% of pages fully correct. - gemini-3.8-flash (think off): 95.6%. - gemini-pro-latest: 93.4%. - Sarvam Vision + Gemini: 92.3%. - Sarvam Vision + 105b: 91.8%. - claude-haiku-5.5: 86.7%. - openai:gpt-5.5: 79.0%. - gpt-5.4-mini: 73.2%. On harsh photos only, gpt-5.5 kept 61% of fields. It produced fluent but invented firm names and GSTINs (for example 'महाराष्ट्र इलेक्ट्रॉनिक्स' for 'महालक्ष्मी एंटरप्राइजेज') rather than leaving fields null. So the most expensive model is not the safest on bad photos.

Caveats

  • The documents are synthetic, computer-rendered pages with system fonts. There are no real stamps, signatures, carbon copies, printer artefacts, folds or Indic handwriting; the 'handwriting' is a Latin handwriting-style font, used only for KYC entries. Real scans will score lower than the clean condition here.
  • The harsh condition covers only 16 pages (kept small to stay inside the Sarvam budget), so its CIs are wide. The direction is clear (Gemini better on every text metric), but the size of the field-accuracy gap is uncertain.
  • Each Sarvam Vision job was given the page's correct language code. A production pipeline has to detect it first.
  • There is one extraction prompt, shared by all systems, and Gemini ran with thinking off. Exact match is strict: names must stay in the printed script, while numbers compare by value and Indic digits are folded to ASCII.
  • Reading order on forms is ambiguous, so the text metric is an order-free CER (described in the README). It does not measure whether the reading order is correct.
  • Gemini prices are not recorded here. Its cost is reported in tokens only.
  • Frontier models ran only on the 30-image subset, and their thinking budgets were the provider defaults (gpt-5.5 reasoning_effort medium, Gemini dynamic, Claude reasoning enabled). OpenAI images went in as data URIs with default detail. OpenAI prices are not recorded, so only tokens are reported.

Use case 4Sarvam behind

Q&A over company documents in Indian languages (RAG)

Employees and customers ask questions (in their own language, in English, or in romanised WhatsApp-style text) over company documents written in Indian languages. Which model answers correctly, in the user's language, and says 'not in the documents' instead of guessing?

uc04 synthetic Indian-language policy documents · n=132 · synthetic, written for this benchmark · licence: CC-BY-4.0 (this repo)

Verdict

For an Indian-language document help-desk, retrieval with gemini-embedding-2 is solved at this scale. Pick the generator for instruction-following. gemini-3.8-flash is the best default in the price-matched tier: 100% correct, 95% English replies to English questions, but only 62% romanised replies to romanised questions. sarvam-105b is fast (0.6 s) and cheap, and nearly always finds the right figure. With thinking off, though, it marks a third of its correct answers as not found and answers English questions in the document's language, so run it with reasoning on (0.96 correct, 3% false refusals, about 5 s) or don't use a refusal tag. Skip sarvam-105b-conversations for this task. gpt-5.4-mini is accurate but almost never answers in the user's language. If users write romanised or English text against Indic documents and language matching matters, only the frontier models (gemini-pro-latest, gpt-5.5, claude-sonnet-5.5) got it right every time on our subset. Whatever the model, scope retrieval to the right organisation: almost every model will quote another company's policy if retrieval hands it one. For on-premise use, qwen3-30b-local reads Indic documents well but over-answers when the documents don't contain the answer and overflows an 8k context on Kannada. sarvam-30b-local tokenizes Indic text efficiently but needs work on its refusal behaviour before it is usable.

Findings

  • Retrieval was not the bottleneck. gemini-embedding-2 put the gold chunk in the top 5 for 108/108 answerable questions (recall@1 0.98), the same for native-script, English and romanised questions. Cross-script search works with the task written into the text (gemini-embedding-2 has no task_type). The corpus is small, though: 39 chunks, each document in a different language.
  • Answer correctness on the full 108 answerable questions (top-5 retrieval): gemini-3.8-flash 1.00, gpt-5.4-mini 0.99, sarvam-105b with thinking 0.96, claude-haiku-5.5 0.94, sarvam-105b with thinking off 0.67, sarvam-105b-conversations 0.52. On the 30-question frontier subset: gemini-pro-latest 1.00, gpt-5.5 0.97, claude-sonnet-5.5 0.97.
  • sarvam-105b with thinking off finds the right number almost every time (gold value present in 98% of replies, 96% for -conversations). It then appends the [NOT_FOUND] tag to 32% of correct answers (47% for -conversations), apparently because some of the 5 excerpts come from other documents. One reply says the answer is in the Periyar bank document, then tags it as not found because it is absent from the Surma Telecom excerpt. A bot that routes on the tag would hide about a third of correct answers. With reasoning on, false refusals fall to 3% and correctness rises to 0.96, at about 8x the latency (p50 4.9 s vs 0.6 s) and 220k reasoning tokens for 240 calls.
  • The oracle condition gives the gold chunk alone, and sarvam-105b with thinking off still scores 0.62. Its errors come from generation and instruction-following, not retrieval. The other systems score the same with or without retrieval.
  • Replying in the user's language is the biggest gap. For native-script questions every system replies in that script (98-100%). For English questions about an Indic document, most models answer in the document's language. Share of English questions answered in English: gpt-5.4-mini 0.07, sarvam-105b 0.11, sarvam-105b-conversations 0.17, claude-haiku-5.5 0.33, sarvam-105b with thinking 0.88, gemini-3.8-flash 0.95, all three frontier models 1.00.
  • Self-hosted models (llama.cpp Q4_K_M, thinking off, all 132 questions, rag condition): qwen3-30b-local answered 0.94 of the 108 answerable questions correctly, but refused only 0.62 of the unanswerable ones and replied in Latin script to 0 of 38 romanised questions. sarvam-30b-local found the gold value in 0.85 of replies, but appended [NOT_FOUND] to 64% of answerable questions (correct 0.30). It answered English questions in English only 5% of the time, refused 0.79 of the unanswerable questions, and is the only system that invented numbers (2 of 132 replies; for example, it made up a ₹1,500 ambulance charge for an unanswerable Kanglish question). sarvam-30b-local is not usable for this task without heavy prompt or format work.
  • Tokenizer cost limits what one machine can serve. The same RAG prompts average 1,900 tokens on Sarvam's tokenizer (105B and 30B), 1,960 on Gemini, 2,320 on gpt-5.4-mini, 5,670 on claude-haiku-5.5 and 6,580 on Qwen3. A Kannada hospital RAG prompt that Sarvam fits in about 1.9k tokens takes 10,088 on Qwen3. On our shared server (32k context split across 4 slots, 8k each) all 14 Kannada prompts overflowed. We reran them on a dedicated 16k-context server so the scores are not distorted; there qwen3 got 0.89 of the Kannada questions right. The lesson: on the same hardware, Qwen3 has 3-5x less context headroom per user for Indic documents than Sarvam.
  • Romanised questions (Hinglish, Tanglish, Manglish, Banglish, Kanglish, romanised Marathi) mostly get native-script replies. Share answered in Latin script: gpt-5.4-mini 0.24, sarvam-105b 0.23, sarvam-105b-conversations 0.31, sarvam-105b with thinking 0.48, gemini-3.8-flash 0.62, claude-haiku-5.5 0.69, frontier models 1.00. On a WhatsApp help-desk most users who type romanised text will get a reply in a script they did not use.
  • Unanswerable questions were refused 88-96% of the time by every system, and no system put an invented number in a reply (hallucinated-number rate 0.00 everywhere). Almost all the failures are one question: a Tamil insurance customer asks about dental cover, and retrieval returns the Hindi HR policy of a different company, which covers dental up to ₹6,500. 8 of 9 cloud systems quoted that ₹6,500 as if it were the insurer's rule (gpt-5.5, claude-sonnet-5.5, gemini-pro-latest, gemini-3.8-flash, gpt-5.4-mini, claude-haiku-5.5, sarvam-105b with thinking, -conversations). sarvam-105b with thinking off named the other company and tagged the answer not found, which is the right call. The general lesson is cross-source contamination: scope retrieval to the right organisation or tenant, because the models will not do it for you.
  • Speed for one RAG answer, p50/p95: sarvam-105b 0.6/5.3 s, -conversations 0.4/4.6 s, gpt-5.4-mini 1.1/1.4 s, claude-haiku-5.5 1.9/2.7 s, gemini-3.8-flash 2.8/5.2 s, sarvam-105b with thinking 4.9/12.8 s.
  • Tokenizer cost differs by provider: the same 240 Indic-language prompts were 313k input tokens on sarvam-105b, 330k on gemini-3.8-flash, 378k on gpt-5.4-mini and 1,002k on claude-haiku-5.5 (3.2x Sarvam).

Caveats

  • The data is synthetic: 6 documents and 132 questions written by an LLM author (Claude). Each gold answer was checked by machine against its chunk, but no native speaker has reviewed the language quality.
  • The task is easy for strong models (several score 1.00), so the differences between systems are about instruction-following (the [NOT_FOUND] tag, reply language) more than reading comprehension. Harder multi-hop or arithmetic questions were deliberately left out.
  • The [NOT_FOUND] tag is our prompt's way to detect refusals. A system that answers correctly and still adds the tag is scored as refusing, because a bot routing on the tag would treat it that way. The lenient metric gold_present_ignoring_tag_rag ignores the tag.
  • The reply-language check uses the dominant script, so a romanised question expects a Latin-script reply. A native-script reply to a romanised question may be acceptable to some users.
  • Only 24 unanswerable questions (12 facts in 2 forms each), so refusal-rate CIs are wide, and one cross-document item accounts for most of the failures.
  • Frontier models ran on a 38-question subset (30 evenly spaced over sorted qids, plus 8 unanswerable), listed in dataset.frontier_subset_qids. Compare them using values_frontier_subset.
  • Local models ran the rag condition on all 132 questions, with no oracle condition. The 14 qwen3-30b-local Kannada prompts that overflowed the shared server's 8k slot were rerun on a temporary dedicated llama-server (-c 16384 -np 1) with the same model and settings. sarvam-30b-local runs with reasoning off via bench.chat's empty-think prefill; its 12 calls made before that fix are excluded. Local latency reflects a shared, loaded Mac and is not a hardware benchmark.

Code: suites/uc04_indic_rag/ · results: results/uc04_indic_rag.json · every output: results/raw/uc04_indic_rag.jsonl

Use case 5Sarvam behind

Mixed-language doctor-patient consultation -> English clinical note

A clinic records an outpatient consultation held in Hinglish / Malayalam-English / Tamil-English / Bengali-English / Marathi-English. Which model turns it into a correct structured English note, and which one invents medicines or doses (the safety risk)?

uc05 synthetic OPD consultations · n=40 · synthetic, written for this benchmark · licence: CC-BY-4.0 (this repo)

Verdict

For an AI scribe working from a transcript, gemini-3.8-flash (thinking off) is the pick in the price-matched tier: perfect on every field we scored, no invented drugs, 4 s per note. gpt-5.4-mini (1.5 s) is a close, faster second. sarvam-105b is as safe (it never invented a medicine) and fast (1.8 s), but it gets about 1 in 15 frequencies wrong, typically turning an as-needed dose into a scheduled one. Reasoning mode does not fix that and makes it 14x slower, so any Sarvam-based scribe needs a frequency check by the doctor. From audio, sending the recording straight to gemini-3.8-flash was the most accurate path in our test (100% on 15 dialogues). The Sarvam pipeline is cheap (₹45/hour of audio with diarization) and diarizes correctly. Use saaras:v4 in codemix mode, then sarvam-105b: on 15 dialogues it scored 0.97 fact recall vs 0.94 for v3 translate, and it fixes v3's spoken-number errors. But every saaras version dropped the same prescription sentence in one Malayalam consultation, and medication exactness stays at 0.83 vs 1.00 for Gemini on the raw audio, so always show the doctor the transcript next to the note. Self-hosted 30B models are not ready to be an unsupervised scribe: about 1 in 5 medicine lines have an error, and 30-40% of notes are not fully in English. qwen3-30b-local was the safer of the two.

Findings

  • From the dialogue text, every cloud model wrote a usable English note. fact_recall_overall over 40 dialogues: gemini-3.8-flash 1.00, gemini-pro-latest 1.00, claude-sonnet-5.5 1.00, gemini-3.8-flash with thinking, gpt-5.4-mini with thinking, claude-haiku-5.5 with thinking and gpt-5.5 all 0.99, sarvam-105b with thinking 0.98, gpt-5.4-mini 0.97, sarvam-105b 0.96 (CI 0.94-0.98), claude-haiku-5.5 without thinking 0.93.
  • Safety metric: no text-track system listed a drug that was not prescribed or a dose that was never said (hallucinated meds/doses per note = 0.00 for all, n=30-40). All 40 traps were handled: refused antibiotics, stopped drugs, self-medication, mid-sentence dose corrections and late-disclosed allergies. With an explicit 'final prescription only' instruction, these models do not invent medicines.
  • The errors that remain are frequency errors, and they are clinically meaningful. 'Paracetamol 5 ml only when fever is above 100, not more than 4 times a day' (an as-needed/SOS dose with a daily cap) was written as scheduled QID or TDS by sarvam-105b (d03, d13), sarvam-105b with thinking (d03, d19, d27, d28), claude-haiku-5.5 (d03, d13, d19, d27, d28), gpt-5.4-mini (d27) and the gpt-4o-transcribe pipeline. sarvam-105b also turned two 'morning one, night one' (BD) prescriptions into OD (d28 cefixime, d31 calcium). Medication exactness (drug + dose + frequency): gemini-3.8-flash 1.00, claude-haiku-5.5 with thinking 1.00, all frontier models 1.00, gpt-5.4-mini 0.99, sarvam-105b 0.93, sarvam-105b with thinking 0.91, claude-haiku-5.5 without thinking 0.90.
  • Writing the note in English is not automatic. Share of notes with no Indic-script text: sarvam-105b, gemini (all modes), the frontier models and all audio pipelines 1.00, gpt-5.4-mini 0.95, claude-haiku-5.5 0.60 (0.90 with thinking), qwen3-30b-local 0.68, sarvam-30b-local 0.58. Claude Haiku and the local models often copied the patient's words in Hindi, Tamil or Bengali into the complaint or red-flag fields, e.g. 'बुखार, पूरे बदन में दर्द…' as the chief complaint.
  • Self-hosted models (Q4_K_M, thinking off, all 40 dialogues), fact recall / medication exactness: qwen3-30b-local 0.79 / 0.87 with 0 invented medicines; sarvam-30b-local 0.78 / 0.79 with one invented medicine (d25: it listed 'Dolo 650' as a second drug next to paracetamol, which could lead to a double paracetamol dose). Neither listed a trap drug as prescribed. Most of their recall loss is complaint and red-flag text left in the source language; vitals recall stays at 0.95-0.97. p50 is 12 s per note on the shared Mac.
  • Thinking did not help sarvam-105b here: medication exactness 0.91 with thinking vs 0.93 without. It cost 173k reasoning tokens for 40 notes, latency rose from 1.8 s to 25.8 s (p50), one note was not valid JSON (d37), and one omitted metformin after a mid-sentence dose correction (d18). For claude-haiku-5.5 and gpt-5.4-mini, thinking did help (0.90 to 1.00, and 0.97 to 0.99 fact recall).
  • Audio track, scored on the same 15 voiced dialogues (fact recall / medication exactness): gemini-3.8-flash directly on the audio 1.00 / 1.00, the same as its text-track score. gpt-4o-transcribe + gpt-5.4-mini 0.98 / 0.90. saaras:v3 translate with diarization + sarvam-105b 0.94 / 0.87, vitals 0.88, red flags 0.74. The note-writer is not the problem: sarvam-105b scores 0.97 / 0.97 on the gold text of those same 15 dialogues, so the STT step costs the Sarvam pipeline about 3 points of fact recall and 10 of medication exactness.
  • saaras:v3 translate-mode errors we saw: (1) d10 Malayalam: the sentence prescribing telmisartan 40 mg was dropped from the transcript entirely ('Both should be eaten regularly' survives, without the drug), so the note lists only amlodipine; this is an omission, not an invented drug. (2) Spoken numbers: Marathi 'one hundred point eight' became 'one hundred and eight' (temperature 108 °F, d35); Tamil 'BP 124 by 80' became 'BP 125' (d17); Marathi 'BP 116 by 74' became '116 divided by 74. What is this reverse multiplication?' (d33). (3) Drug spelling: 'Glimipride' for glimepiride (d26). Diarization was right at the coarse level: 2 speakers in 15/15 files, and the median ratio of detected to scripted speaker changes was 1.0.
  • saaras:v4 (released 25 Sep 2026) on the same 15 dialogues, same diarized batch API, note by sarvam-105b. Fact recall / medication exactness / red-flag recall: v3 translate 0.94 / 0.87 / 0.74; v4 translate 0.93 / 0.83 / 0.86; v4 codemix (source-language transcript with English terms kept, then sarvam-105b translates) 0.97 / 0.83 / 0.93. v4 fixes the spoken-decimal error: Marathi 'one hundred point eight' now comes out as 100.8, not 108 (d35). It does not fix the dropped prescription: in d10 all three saaras variants omit the sentence 'with it, Telmisartan 40 mg once a day at night' that comes right after the diagnosis sentence, while gpt-4o-transcribe has it word for word, so the sentence is in the audio. v4 translate added new errors: it lost a dose correction (d02 glimepiride 2 mg instead of the corrected 1 mg), garbled glimepiride as 'Gimi Pride', which is scored as an unsupported medicine (0.07 per note), and read 'BP 124 by 80' as 'BP 120' (d17). v4 codemix had no unsupported medicines and is the best Sarvam audio pipeline here, though medication exactness (0.83) is still below gpt-4o-transcribe + gpt-5.4-mini (0.90) and Gemini direct (1.00). The 95% CIs overlap heavily with n=15. Diarization: 2 speakers detected in 15/15 files for both v4 modes. The model name 'saaras:v4-multispk' is rejected with HTTP 400 'deprecated, use saaras-multispeaker'; plain 'saaras:v4' accepts with_diarization=true and returns diarized_transcript. Batch jobs still took about 10 s, and outputs are still named by upload index.
  • saaras:v3 batch quirk: output files are named by upload index ('0.json', '1.json', ...), not after the input file. Two jobs downloaded into one folder overwrite each other, so map outputs via job_details[i].inputs/outputs from the status endpoint. Our first run lost 12 of 15 transcripts this way. Batch jobs of 3 files (about 70 s of audio each) finished in 10-11 s.
  • gemini-3.8-flash-tts multi-speaker requires each text part to carry speech_metadata.speaker. A single prompt with 'Doctor: … Patient: …' lines is rejected with HTTP 400. 15 dialogues produced 1,081 s of audio. Every gold dose number appears in at least one of the two STT transcripts, so the TTS did not drop doses.
  • Separately, asking gemini-3.8-flash for a verbatim transcript of d01 left out the first three turns, although the audio contains them (a clip of the first 15 s transcribes fine). Its notes from audio were still complete, so this affects plain transcription only.
  • Speed per note, p50/p95: gpt-5.4-mini 1.5/1.9 s, sarvam-105b 1.8/2.2 s, claude-haiku-5.5 2.5/3.4 s, gemini-3.8-flash 4.4/13.3 s, gemini-3.8-flash with thinking 13.8/23.1 s, sarvam-105b with thinking 25.8/45.5 s. Audio: saaras batch (about 10 s per job) then sarvam-105b at 2.2 s; Gemini audio-to-note in one call at 5.7 s.

Caveats

  • The 40 dialogues and gold facts are synthetic, written by an LLM author (Claude). They are clean and well-structured compared with real OPD talk: no crosstalk, no background noise, every vital stated clearly. The task is near the ceiling for strong models.
  • The audio is TTS (2 studio voices, no noise, no overlap), so the STT and audio results are optimistic compared with a real clinic recording. Recorded consultations with consent would be the next step.
  • Free-text fields (complaint, diagnosis, red flags, follow-up) are scored by alias word overlap with a small synonym map. Correct paraphrases can still be marked as misses, so absolute red-flag recall is understated. All systems are scored with the same matcher, and we audited the misses by hand.
  • The 'hallucinated dose' check only catches dose numbers that never appear in the dialogue. A real but wrong dose taken from elsewhere in the conversation shows up as a medication-exactness error instead.
  • Frontier models ran on 30 of 40 dialogues (evenly spread across languages; dataset.frontier_subset_ids). Local models ran all 40 text dialogues. Use values_frontier_subset / values_audio_subset to compare like with like.
  • n is small (40 notes, 15 audio, 13 dialogues with allergies), so CIs are wide. sarvam-105b's medication exactness CI is 0.85-0.99.

Code: suites/uc05_clinical_notes/ · results: results/uc05_clinical_notes.json · every output: results/raw/uc05_clinical_notes.jsonl

Use case 6Level

Offline crop advisory

Can an open-weight model running on a local box (no internet, possibly no GPU) answer farmers' questions correctly from an advisory sheet, in their own language and script?

uc06 advisory sheet + farmer questions · n=70 · synthetic, written for this benchmark · licence: CC-BY-4.0 (this repo)

Verdict

Neither open-weight 30B model is safe as an unsupervised offline crop advisor in this setup. With thinking off, they give the right numbers for only ~70% of sheet questions and, worse, invent answers to most questions the sheet does not cover. Thinking on stops most of the invention but takes minutes per answer on shared hardware and produces more wrong-language replies. The two models tie on accuracy. Sarvam-30B replies in the farmer's language more reliably and processes Indic prompts with fewer tokens, so prefer it if you must go offline, behind a retrieval or whitelist layer and code checks that every number in an answer appears in the sheet. If there is any connectivity, use gemini-3.8-flash (100% grounded, no inventions) or sarvam-105b (95% grounded, 100% correct language, sub-second, ~₹0.02 per answer). The frontier models are perfect on the subset. Avoid gpt-5.4-mini and claude-haiku-5.5 for this job: they don't invent answers, but they refuse a quarter of answerable farmer questions.

Findings

  • Grounded correctness on the 60 in-scope questions (answer contains every gold number from the sheet): gemini-3.8-flash 100%, sarvam-105b 95% [90,100]. Every offline variant lands at 68-77% with overlapping CIs: Sarvam-30B 73% (without thinking, with thinking, and on CPU alike), Qwen3-30B-A3B 68% without thinking, 77% with, 73% on CPU.
  • The big offline risk is invented answers. Without thinking, Sarvam-30B refuses only 1 of 10 out-of-scope questions (3/10 if a helpline redirect without the code counts) and Qwen3 refuses 0/10 (4/10 lenient). Examples: Sarvam told a Tamil farmer to use 150 kg DAP per acre on tomato, and Qwen3 told a Marathi farmer that soybean is ₹1,800 per quintal today. Neither appears in the sheet.
  • Cloud comparators (ADDENDUM). Cloud models do NOT invent answers to out-of-scope questions: gpt-5.4-mini, claude-haiku-5.5, gemini-pro-latest, gpt-5.5 and claude-sonnet-5.5 all refused 10/10. But the cheap ones over-refuse real sheet questions: gpt-5.4-mini answered 'NOT_IN_SHEET' to 23% of in-scope questions and claude-haiku-5.5 to 27%. This happened mostly on romanised or farmer-vocabulary phrasings (e.g. 'kandu jigihulu' for brown planthopper, 'ਨਰਮਾ' for cotton). As a result their grounded correctness, 75% and 70%, is no better than the offline 30B models. gpt-5.4-mini also mixes English into native-script replies ('40 kg प्रति acre'), so only 79% of its replies are in the farmer's language. On the fixed 30-question subset (all 10 out-of-scope + 20 in-scope), all three frontier models pass 30/30. On the same subset gemini-3.8-flash passes 93% and sarvam-105b 90%. gpt-5.4-mini and claude-haiku-5.5 pass 70%. Offline: Sarvam-30B 50% and Qwen3 40% without thinking; 60% each with thinking.
  • Thinking fixes most of the invention (out-of-scope refusal: Sarvam-30B 100%, Qwen3 90%) but costs a lot. Sarvam-30B produced 1,577 output tokens per answer (p50 198 s on the shared GPU). False refusals rise to 13% (Sarvam) and 8% (Qwen3). Sarvam-30B's correct-language replies fall from 96% to 76%.
  • Replying in the farmer's language and script, without thinking: Sarvam-30B 96% [90,100], Qwen3 90% [81,97], sarvam-105b 100%, Gemini 96%. Romanised questions are harder for every offline model: Sarvam-30B 67% grounded (native 80%), Qwen3 57% (native 80%). Several replies switched to native script or to English.
  • Offline accuracy depends heavily on language. Overall pass, Sarvam-30B no-think: Hindi 83%, Marathi 83%, Tamil 82%, Kannada 58%, Punjabi 36%, Telugu 33%. sarvam-105b on the same questions: 100/100/100/92/91/75%.
  • CPU-only box (6 threads, the sheet's KV prefix reused across questions): Sarvam-30B p50 22 s / p95 49 s per answer, Qwen3 p50 19 s / p95 98 s, with the same accuracy as on GPU. The first (cold) question took 217 s, because processing the 1,471-token sheet runs at 7.7 tok/s. Qwen3 needs more tokens for the same Indic question and answer (uc12), which shows in its longer tail.
  • sarvam-105b online: p50 0.48 s, 95% grounded, 100% correct language, out-of-scope 8/10 with the NOT_IN_SHEET code and 10/10 counting helpline redirects. List cost for all 70 answers ₹1.68 (103k input tokens, mostly the sheet).
  • OpenRouter quirks: one claude-haiku-5.5 Kannada reply came back as mojibake (UTF-8 decoded as Latin-1, e.g. 'Ī£ÅļĖÅ ß▓ēß▓Š...'), and one leaked its reasoning into the answer ('Question is in Telugu (Telugu script? No, it's Latin letters...').

Caveats

  • One synthetic sheet and 70 hand-written questions (not native-reviewed). CIs are about ±10 points; per-language cells have 10-12 items.
  • 'Grounded correct' checks that the gold numbers are present. It cannot catch a correct number attached to the wrong crop or unit, so it is an upper bound.
  • The strict out-of-scope metric requires the NOT_IN_SHEET code. The lenient variant also accepts a KVK/helpline redirect; both are reported.
  • The CPU and GPU runs used a shared Mac under heavy load (load average 15-560), so latencies are pessimistic. CPU answers ran one at a time with llama.cpp's prompt cache, which is how a single kiosk would behave.
  • Sarvam Edge (Sarvam's on-device stack) is not publicly downloadable, so it was not tested. Only the official Q4_K_M GGUF of Sarvam-30B was tested.
  • Frontier systems ran only on SUBSET: all 10 out-of-scope questions plus every 3rd fact, native and romanised (20 in-scope). Compare them with the *_subset30 metrics.

Code: suites/uc06_offline_agri/ · results: results/uc06_offline_agri.json · every output: results/raw/uc06_offline_agri.jsonl

Use case 7Level

Translation and dubbing of training content / product copy

Localising training content and product copy into Indian languages, then dubbing it: which translation system and which TTS should an Indian business use?

FLEURS test transcriptions (= FLORES-101 sentences) aligned by id · n=32 · public data · licence: CC-BY 4.0

Verdict

For localising formal English content into Indian languages, use sarvam-translate:v1. It was the most accurate system into Indian languages in 8 of 10 languages, and on a small subset no frontier model (gemini-pro, gpt-5.5, claude-sonnet-5.5) did better. Its lead over mayura:v1 and gemini-3.8-flash is only about 2 chrF, and it costs about 80x more per item than prompting sarvam-105b, so high-volume, lower-stakes copy can go through 105b or a price-matched model. For Indian languages into English (customer feedback, regional documents), use gemini-3.8-flash or claude-haiku-5.5. They lead sarvam-translate by 10-12 chrF, and sarvam-translate makes meaning-changing errors in that direction. Use mayura's colloquial mode only when you want code-mixed copy. For dubbing, bulbul:v3, gemini-3.8-flash-tts and gpt-4o-mini-tts are all intelligible in all 10 languages, with bulbul and Gemini slightly ahead. Bulbul starts playback about 3x sooner (357 ms) and has a simple per-character rupee price, so it is the best default for interactive voice and a fine choice for batch voice-overs. The self-hosted 30B models are not ready for production translation into Indian languages.

Findings

  • English->Indic, full set (320 items per system): sarvam-translate:v1 has the highest chrF++, 51.8 [50.1-53.5]. Next are mayura:v1 49.8, gemini-3.8-flash 49.7, claude-haiku-5.5 47.8, gpt-5.4-mini 46.6 and sarvam-105b 45.6. sarvam-translate is best of these systems in 8 of 10 languages (Gemini wins Kannada, Haiku wins Malayalam).
  • Frontier models do not beat sarvam-translate into Indian languages. On the 30 sentence-language pairs where every system ran, sarvam-translate scores 53.5 against gemini-pro-latest 51.9, gemini-3.8-flash 51.9, gpt-5.5 51.0 and claude-sonnet-5.5 51.0, all with thinking on. The CIs (about +/-5 points at n=30) overlap, so the honest reading is 'no better', not 'worse'.
  • Indic->English ranks the other way round: gemini-3.8-flash 64.3 [62.5-66.2], claude-haiku-5.5 62.1, gpt-5.4-mini 60.4, sarvam-105b 57.8, mayura 54.6, sarvam-translate:v1 52.5. On the 30-pair frontier subset, claude-sonnet-5.5 scores 65.9, about level with gemini-3.8-flash at 62.8. sarvam-translate's errors into English change the meaning. Hindi 'fabric ... shrinkage, or scorch' became 'clothing ... could lead to hypothermia or even burns', and Tamil 'appeared in court with covered faces' became 'was present in the court in the dock'.
  • Cost differs by about 80x for similar volume. sarvam-105b translated all 640 items for about INR 1.4 in tokens (34.5k in, 15.3k out). sarvam-translate and mayura each cost about INR 115 at INR 20 per 10k input chars (57.8k chars). claude-haiku-5.5 cost US$0.029 for the same 640 items, as reported by OpenRouter.
  • mayura:v1 modern-colloquial mode produces Hinglish/Tanglish copy: 61% of output letters are Latin, e.g. 'Fabric ரொம்ப hot ஆகாம பாத்துக்கோங்க'. Against the formal reference it scores chrF++ 16 vs 49 for formal mode. That is a deliberate change of register, not an error, and suits chat or marketing copy rather than formal training material.
  • Dubbing intelligibility (26 sentences x 6 languages per TTS, three STT judges): bulbul:v3 and gemini-3.8-flash-tts are statistically tied, and gpt-4o-mini-tts is slightly behind. CER with saaras:v3 as judge: bulbul 1.8%, Gemini 1.9%, OpenAI 2.4%. With the vendor-neutral gpt-4o-transcribe as judge: Gemini 3.5%, bulbul 4.3%, OpenAI 5.0%, CIs overlapping. With Gemini as judge, counting its refusals as failures: Gemini 5.9%, OpenAI 6.7%, bulbul 7.3%. Without the refusals those three are 2.8%, 2.3% and 2.3%.
  • Judge bias is small and not consistent. The neutral OpenAI judge slightly favours Gemini TTS. Saaras slightly favours bulbul. The Gemini judge refused bulbul audio most often (8 refusals vs 5 for its own TTS), and once refusals are excluded it scores bulbul and OpenAI best. Every TTS stays under about 5% CER with every judge.
  • Bulbul is fastest to first audio. Streaming TTFB p50 is 357 ms for bulbul, 991 ms for gpt-4o-mini-tts and 1154 ms for Gemini TTS. The full clip arrives at p50 1.69 s, 2.06 s and 2.89 s respectively. In a 2-call spot check, Bulbul's non-streaming REST endpoint took 5.8-7.6 s for the same text, so use the stream endpoint.
  • TTS cost per 10k characters: bulbul:v3 INR 30 (list price). gpt-4o-mini-tts about US$0.23, estimated from audio minutes at about $0.015/min. Gemini TTS used about 19.4k audio output tokens; no Gemini price is assumed. All three TTS produced audio in all 10 languages tested.
  • The local 30B models trail the APIs on the 8-sentence subset. Into Indian languages, sarvam-30b-local scores 37.8 and qwen3-30b-local 36.0, against about 45-50 for the cloud systems. Into English they score 55.2 and 53.4, close to mayura. sarvam-30b-local returned the English source untranslated in 9 of 80 English->Indic items (e.g. 'Lions are the most social cats...' in bn, ta, kn, pa), and added an unrequested extra paragraph once. Qwen3 always produced the target script.

Caveats

  • chrF++ uses a single human reference per sentence. A correct paraphrase loses points, so differences under about 2 points on the full set, or about 5 points on 30-item subsets, are noise (see CIs).
  • FLEURS/FLORES sentences are general prose (news, travel, science), not real product copy or training modules. Brand names, UI strings and domain glossaries were not tested.
  • Test-set sizes are small. Price-matched systems ran 32 sentences x 10 languages x 2 directions (320 items per direction); the size was capped by the Sarvam translate price. Frontier models (thinking on) ran only sentence ids 1669, 1672 and 1701 x 10 languages x 2 directions (30 pairs per direction). Local models ran the first 8 sentences, because the shared llama-server was saturated (p95 latency up to 99 s). Compare systems only within the subset metrics.
  • LLM systems got a plain one-line translation prompt with no glossary. Before scoring, every system's output is cut to its first paragraph, so an unrequested 'Explanation' section does not count against chrF; this mattered for one sarvam-30b-local reply. Sarvam-30B runs with thinking off by prefilling an empty think block.
  • Dubbing measures intelligibility only, not naturalness, prosody, voice/gender fit or pronunciation of English loanwords. Sentences containing digits were excluded (26 remained). Voices: bulbul one named voice per language, Gemini Kore, OpenAI alloy plus a one-line 'read in <language>' instruction.
  • Gemini-judge refusals count as failures (CER 1.0): 20 of 504 benign transcription requests were blocked with BlockedReason.OTHER (bulbul 8, OpenAI 7, Gemini 5). This inflates the Gemini-judge CERs, and the finding also gives the numbers without refusals. gpt-4o-transcribe rejected the language hints 'pa' and 'or' (HTTP 400), so those 18 clips were transcribed without a hint.
  • During the run, Sarvam credits ran out once and many calls hit the shared 429 rate limit. Failed calls were retried and none are scored.
  • Spend for this suite: Sarvam about INR 328 (translate 231, bulbul 46, saaras about 32, 105b 1.4). OpenAI tokens and audio are recorded in usage; the TTS and transcribe estimates come to about US$0.73, and the chat models used a few cents. OpenRouter cost about US$0.09 as reported.

Code: suites/uc07_translation_dubbing/ · results: results/uc07_translation_dubbing.json · every output: results/raw/uc07_translation_dubbing.jsonl

Use case 8Level

Code-mixed quick-commerce orders and product/place-name transliteration

Can a model turn code-mixed WhatsApp/quick-commerce order and search messages into a correct structured order, and write Indian names in native script correctly?

uc08 hand-authored orders (100) + transliteration names (100) · n=200 · synthetic, written for this benchmark · licence: CC-BY 4.0

Verdict

To turn WhatsApp-style code-mixed orders into structured carts, gemini-3.8-flash with thinking off is the best value. It got 98% of whole orders exactly right in about 3 s and was within the CI of the frontier models (gpt-5.5 100% and gemini-pro 97% on a 30-message subset). claude-haiku-5.5 (85%) is a reasonable second choice. sarvam-105b is usable only with thinking on (90-91% exact). Even then it takes 9 s p50 and 23-27 s p95, and it needs a max_tokens of 16k plus a retry on empty replies. Without thinking it confuses regional grocery words and should not write orders unsupervised. Every cloud model reads pincode and payment correctly, so those fields are safe to automate today. For writing names in native script (labels, invoices, search), use gemini-3.8-flash, claude-haiku-5.5 or gpt-5.4-mini (96-99%). The Sarvam transliterate API is cheap and fast for Hindi and Marathi but makes visible errors on Tamil and Bengali names. The local 30B models are not yet good enough for either task without a catalog-mapping layer.

Findings

  • Order extraction, exact whole-order accuracy over 100 code-mixed messages. Thinking off: gemini-3.8-flash 98% [95-100], claude-haiku-5.5 85%, gpt-5.4-mini 77%, sarvam-105b 71% [62-80]. With thinking, sarvam-105b reaches 90-91%. Strict item F1 for the same systems is 0.99, 0.92, 0.89, 0.85 and 0.95 (105b-think with the 16k cap). On the 50-message local subset, qwen3-30b-local scores 36% exact.
  • On the fixed 30-message frontier subset (ids with (id-1)%10 in {0,3,6}, covering every language group), exact accuracy with thinking on is gpt-5.5 100%, gemini-pro-latest 97% and claude-sonnet-5.5 93%. Price-matched systems on the same messages: gemini-3.8-flash 93%, claude-haiku-5.5 90%, sarvam-105b-think 87% (16k cap), gpt-5.4-mini 63%, sarvam-105b 63%. gemini-3.8-flash with thinking off is within the CI of the frontier ceiling.
  • sarvam-105b without thinking makes regional-vocabulary mistakes, not format mistakes. Bengali 'sorsher tel' (mustard oil) became sesame oil, Tamil 'sakkarai' (sugar) became jaggery, Tamil 'theangai' (coconut) became banana, and 'sona masoori' became basmati rice. It also drops brands written in Tamil script (மேகி -> no brand), treats varieties as brands (Ponni, alphonso), sets search quantities to 1 packet instead of '200g', and invents slot labels ('night', 'evening_16-20') on 6% of messages. Its catalog-name F1 is still 0.98: it finds the products but gets the details wrong.
  • sarvam-105b thinking can return nothing. At max_tokens 6000, 3 of 100 replies (ids 18, 74, 99) came back empty after spending the whole budget on reasoning. Rerun at 16000, all 3 answered correctly, using about 3.8k completion tokens each, below the earlier cap. The reasoning length is non-deterministic, not simply too long for the cap. docs-legal saw the same pattern (16 of 80 empty), so any 105b-think deployment needs a high max_tokens and a retry on empty content. Exact accuracy goes from 90% to 91%, p95 latency stays at 23-27 s, and reasoning averages about 1,700 tokens per message.
  • Pincode and payment extraction is solved for every cloud model: 100% for gemini-3.8-flash, gpt-5.4-mini, claude-haiku-5.5, sarvam-105b and all three frontier models. That includes pincodes in Bengali (৭০০০৬৪), Devanagari (४११०३८) and Kannada (೫೬೦೦೧೧) digits, and slang such as GPay/PhonePe/Paytm/nakad/'cash e debo'. Gemini 3.8 Flash's only 2 misses wrote the brand in Devanagari (मैगी, हल्दीराम), which a catalog lookup would not match.
  • qwen3-30b-local copies the customer's word instead of mapping it to the catalog (bhindi, gajar, theangai, pauruti, Bisleri, Pampers instead of okra, carrot, coconut, bread, packaged water, diapers), so name-only F1 is 0.72. It is fast (p50 5.5 s on the shared Mac) and always produced valid JSON.
  • Transliteration exact match over 100 names: gemini-3.8-flash 99%, claude-haiku-5.5 97%, gpt-5.4-mini 96%, sarvam-105b 89%, Sarvam /transliterate API 88%. On the 30-name frontier subset, gemini-pro-latest, gpt-5.5 and claude-sonnet-5.5 all score 100%. On the 50-name local subset, qwen3-30b-local scores 66%. The Sarvam API is strong in Hindi and Marathi (96%) and weak in Tamil (76%). Examples: Tiruchirappalli became திருச்சிற்றம்பலம் (a different place), Kavitha became கவிதை (the word 'poem'), Rameswaram became a mixed-script 'ரameswaram', and Bankura became বঙ্গুরা.
  • Marathi orthography separates the models: sarvam-105b wrote गोकुल and शिवजी where Marathi uses गोकुळ and शिवाजी. Gemini 3.8 Flash, gpt-5.4-mini and claude-haiku-5.5 got all 25 Marathi names right, including ळ in लोणावळा and महाबळेश्वर.
  • Cost and speed: the Sarvam transliterate API costs INR 20 per 10k chars (about INR 2 for 100 names) at p50 0.72 s. sarvam-105b order extraction costs about INR 1.8 per 100 orders without thinking and about INR 12 with thinking. claude-haiku-5.5 cost US$0.016 per 100 orders (OpenRouter-reported). gpt-5.4-mini is fastest at p50 1.07 s per order, but at 77% exact it is the least accurate cloud model here.

Caveats

  • All data is synthetic and was written by one author: 100 messages and 100 names. 95% CIs are about +/-8 points at n=100 and +/-10-15 at n=30. Some golds are judgement calls (for example '1 kg sorsher tel' accepts kg or l, and 'aaj raat tak' is today_night); they are written down in build_data.py.
  • Four Bengali transliteration golds gained accepted variants after the first outputs were seen: native surname forms (Bose -> বসু, Chatterjee -> চট্টোপাধ্যায়), অরিজিত beside অরিজিৎ, and ঋতুপর্ণ (used for both genders). Before that change, exact match was Sarvam API 84%, sarvam-105b 88%, gemini 98%.
  • The strict brand check requires a Latin-script brand matching the catalog. A brand returned in native script (मैगी) counts as wrong, because the downstream catalog lookup would fail too.
  • 'sarvam-105b-think' is the original run with max_tokens 6000, where empty replies are scored as failures. 'sarvam-105b-think(16k cap)' is the same run with the 3 empty replies replaced by their 16k reruns. Both are reported.
  • Frontier models ran with thinking on and only on the fixed 30-message and 30-name subsets (every id with index%10 in {0,3,6}). Price-matched cloud models ran with thinking off on the full sets.
  • Local models were scored on subsets (every other message and every other name) because the shared llama-server was saturated. sarvam-30b-local ran at 2-6 minutes per call and had finished fewer than 20 items when this was written. Its numbers are placeholders and get updated automatically if the background run completes.
  • Spend for this suite: Sarvam about INR 16. OpenRouter about US$0.14 as reported. OpenAI used about 95k input and 14k output tokens across gpt-5.4-mini and gpt-5.5, well under budget; tokens are in usage.

Code: suites/uc08_quick_commerce/ · results: results/uc08_quick_commerce.json · every output: results/raw/uc08_quick_commerce.jsonl

Use case 9Level

Courts and legal: translating and summarising judgments without losing facts

If I translate or summarise English court orders, RTI replies and tribunal awards into Hindi, Tamil, Marathi or Bengali for litigants, which system keeps every amount, date, section, case number and party name intact?

uc09-synthetic-legal-passages · n=40 · synthetic, written for this benchmark · licence: CC0 (synthetic)

Verdict

For translating court orders, RTI replies and tribunal awards into Hindi, Tamil, Marathi or Bengali, gemini-3.8-flash, sarvam-105b (think off) and sarvam-translate:v1 all keep about 99.5% or more of the facts. Hindi is essentially solved, and Tamil is where they differ. If you want a Sarvam stack, prefer sarvam-105b: it matched sarvam-translate on facts at roughly 1/80th of the list cost per passage. Do not use mayura:v1 for legal or financial text: it loses about one fact in every two passages and garbles decimal crore amounts (₹25.5 crore became 5 crore). For plain-language litigant summaries, every non-Sarvam cloud model tested (gemini-3.8-flash, gpt-5.4-mini, claude-haiku-5.5, and the frontier tier on its subset) is clearly better: 98% of key facts and no invented numbers, against 85% and 9% of summaries with unsupported numbers for sarvam-105b. If you use sarvam-105b, either keep thinking off or give it at least 16k max_tokens (89% recall at about 20x the tokens and 21 s); tell it not to compute dates or totals, and check every number in the output against the source before it reaches a litigant. Self-hosted, qwen3-30b did better than sarvam-30b on this small sample.

Findings

  • Translation, share of source facts preserved (120 passage-language items each): gemini-3.8-flash 99.8% [99.6, 100], sarvam-105b (think off) 99.6% [99.3, 99.9], sarvam-translate:v1 99.5% [99.1, 99.8], mayura:v1 96.2% [95.1, 97.3]. Facts dropped or altered per passage: 0.025 / 0.058 / 0.075 / 0.53. Every system wrote 100% of outputs in the target script.
  • Hindi is nearly solved: no facts were lost by any system except mayura (0.1 per passage). Tamil is hardest. Dropped or altered facts per Tamil passage: mayura 0.68, sarvam-105b 0.18, sarvam-translate 0.13, gemini 0.05. Marathi and Bengali sit in between, with mayura at 0.9 and 0.75.
  • mayura:v1 alters money and identifiers, and it is the only system that lost amounts at a meaningful rate (93.5% preserved vs at least 99.6% for the others). With a decimal crore amount it keeps only the digits after the point, in every language: ₹25.5 crore became '5 करोड़', '5 கோடி', '5 कोटी' and '5 কোটি', and ₹15.4 and ₹14.8 crore became 4 and 8 crore. That happened in 10 of 10 decimal-crore cases; the whole-number ₹20 crore was kept. It dropped cheque numbers and Act years. One Tamil passage got stuck repeating a sentence about 10 times. It changed a party's name (Rajendra Prasad Yadav became ராஜசேகர பிரசாத் யாதவ்). In one order it labelled both parties 'accused'.
  • sarvam-translate:v1 altered 1 number in 120 items: cheque no. 493369 became '4933/69' in Bengali. Otherwise it matched the LLMs.
  • Cost per 650-character passage at Sarvam list prices: the translate APIs cost about ₹1.25 (₹20 per 10k characters). sarvam-105b costs about ₹0.016 (about 230 input and 215 output tokens), roughly 80x cheaper, with equal or better fact preservation. Latency p50: mayura 1.5 s, sarvam-105b 1.5 s, sarvam-translate 1.8 s, gemini 3.7 s.
  • Litigant summaries, key-fact recall (80 items each, 6 facts per item): gemini-3.8-flash 98.3% [96.9, 99.4], sarvam-105b think off 85.2% [81.5, 88.7], think on 72.1% [63.5, 80.4]. Mostly sarvam-105b omits dates and case or FIR numbers: by type it kept 77% of dates, 81% of numbers and 91% of amounts, against Gemini's 100% / 96% / 100%.
  • sarvam-105b (think off) put numbers that are not in the order into 9% of summaries (0.125 distinct per summary; 0.25 in Tamil, 0 in Hindi). These were mostly values it computed itself: deadline dates like '58 days, i.e. by 28 March 2024', and summed totals. A litigant who acts on a wrong computed date is harmed. Gemini and think-on put no such numbers in their summaries.
  • Turning sarvam-105b thinking on (reasoning_effort medium) with max_tokens 6000 returned empty content on 16 of 80 replies, because reasoning used up the budget (about 4,250 reasoning tokens on average), which gave 72.1% key-fact recall. Rerunning just those 16 at max_tokens 16000 gave real answers for all 16; they used 2.5k-6.7k reasoning tokens, which shows the reasoning length varies run to run. With the reruns, think-on scores 89.4% [85.8, 92.7] with 0.025 unsupported numbers per summary, against 85.2% and 0.125 for think-off. The cost is p50 latency of 21 s instead of 1.4 s and about 20x the output tokens. Both numbers are in the results (systems 'sarvam-105b-think' and 'sarvam-105b-think (empties rerun at 16k)').
  • Local models, run only on 5 passages x Hindi/Tamil (10 items) on a shared, loaded Mac: - qwen3-30b-local: 90% key-fact recall, no unsupported numbers, 100% in the target language, about 38 s per summary. - sarvam-30b-local, rerun with the shared think-prefill fix and a 1,500-token cap: 83% recall, 1.1 unsupported numbers per summary (such as truncated '₹13,80,00' and case no. '27779' for 2779), and 70% in the target language. All 10 replies ran to the 1,500-token cap. It appends unrequested 'Note' or 'Final, very simple explanation' sections, repeats blocks, and once answered entirely in English. Each reply took about 2-3 min.
  • Translation, price-matched cloud tier (120 items each): openai:gpt-5.4-mini kept 99.9% of facts (0.008 lost per passage) and claude-haiku-5.5 kept 99.9% (0.017). Both are slightly ahead of gemini-3.8-flash (99.8%) and sarvam-105b (99.6%), and none added unsupported numbers. Frontier models on the fixed 30 items (first 15 passages x hi/ta): gpt-5.5 100%, claude-sonnet-5.5 99.8%, gemini-pro-latest 99.8%. On that same subset, sarvam-translate scored 99.5% and sarvam-105b 99.3%. Translation is close to solved for every system except mayura.
  • Litigant summaries, key-fact recall: - Price-matched tier (80 items each): gpt-5.4-mini 97.5%, claude-haiku-5.5 97.3%, gemini-3.8-flash 98.3%; none invented numbers. - Frontier, same 30 items: gpt-5.5 100%, claude-sonnet-5.5 100%, gemini-pro-latest 97.8%. - On those 30 items, sarvam-105b scored 84.4% with think off and 92.8% with think on (reruns included). So the Sarvam API is the only cloud option that leaves out roughly 1 in 7 key facts.
  • The OpenAI models sometimes answer in mixed Hindi-English: gpt-5.4-mini in 1 of 80 summaries and gpt-5.5 in 1 of 30. They keep court names, 'Criminal Complaint No.' and party names in Latin script, so less than 50% of the letters are Devanagari. That fails the language check even though the facts are all there.
  • Latency p50: translation gpt-5.4-mini 2.0 s, claude-haiku 3.5 s, claude-sonnet 5.3 s, gpt-5.5 14 s, gemini-pro 23 s. Summaries gpt-5.4-mini 2.0 s, haiku 3.5 s, sonnet 8.5 s, gpt-5.5 9.6 s, gemini-pro 16 s.

Caveats

  • The passages are synthetic: 12 templates filled 40 times, so errors are correlated within a template. Real judgments are longer, messier and full of citations. The source is always English.
  • Scoring checks whether entities survive, not meaning. Swapped party roles, wrong outcomes (bail granted or rejected) and negations are not caught. Spot checks found such errors (mayura calling both parties 'accused'). The examples in this file show full outputs.
  • The name check is a heuristic: a consonant skeleton with fuzzy matching (see score.py). Correct Tamil spellings that write h as க (சவுகான் for Chauhan) are missed, and modernised place names (Madras to சென்னை, Bombay to मुंबई) count as altered. Both affect every system. Amounts written fully in words are not credited.
  • The LLMs were told to keep numbers and write names in the target script. The translate APIs cannot take instructions and ran with defaults (formal mode, international numerals).
  • Think-on ran with max_tokens 6000. With a larger budget it would return fewer empty replies, at higher cost and latency.
  • The local-model results rest on 10 items and are indicative only. Their latency reflects a shared machine running other jobs. sarvam-30b-local's reasoning leak may come from the llama.cpp chat-template setup rather than the model.
  • Back-translation was not run. Translation fluency and legal register were not measured.
  • Frontier models ran only on a fixed 30-item subset per task (first 15 passages x Hindi/Tamil), with think on at provider-default effort. OpenAI prices are not recorded; OpenRouter cost is what usage.cost reported.
