Use case 10Sarvam behind

Self-hosting Sarvam-30B for business text

Can an Indian business run Sarvam-30B on its own hardware instead of a cloud API, and what does it give up in accuracy and speed?

uc10 synthetic support & back-office set · n=150 · synthetic, written for this benchmark · licence: CC-BY-4.0 (this repo)

Verdict

Self-hosting Sarvam-30B works on a 128 GB Mac-class box: about 21 GB of memory, ~27 tok/s single-stream and a 1 s first token on a 1k-token Indic prompt. That is faster than Qwen3-30B-A3B, largely because its tokenizer needs 2.4x fewer tokens for the same Indic text. But the official Q4_K_M build is the least accurate system tested on Indian back-office tasks: 63% fully correct vs 84% for Qwen3-30B-A3B without thinking and 91% with it. Its failures are about following output instructions, not understanding the text. If data must stay on-premises, Qwen3-30B-A3B (thinking on for accuracy, off for latency) is the better self-hosted choice today. Use Sarvam-30B only where its Indic token efficiency matters and code validates every output. If an API is allowed, any price-matched cloud model is clearly better: gemini-3.8-flash 100%, gpt-5.4-mini 99%, claude-haiku-5.5 96%, sarvam-105b with reasoning off 94% (₹0.87 per 150 items, 0.6 s). Keep 105B reasoning off for structured outputs. A GPU-less CPU box is only viable for overnight batch work.

Findings

  • Fully-correct rate over 150 items (95% CI): gemini-3.8-flash 100% [100,100]; sarvam-105b reasoning off 94% [90,97]; Qwen3-30B-A3B local with thinking 91% [87,95], without 84% [77,89]; sarvam-105b reasoning on 80% [73,86]; Sarvam-30B local without thinking 63% [55,70], with thinking 61% [53,69]. Self-hosted Sarvam-30B trails the same-class Qwen3-30B-A3B by 21 points (no-think vs no-think) and the CIs do not overlap.
  • Cloud comparators added later (ADDENDUM). Price-matched tier, full 150 items, thinking off: openai:gpt-5.4-mini 99%, claude-haiku-5.5 96% (p50 0.9 s and 1.5 s). Frontier tier, thinking on, fixed 30-item subset (6 per task, one per language): gemini-pro-latest 100%, claude-sonnet-5.5 100%, gpt-5.5 97% (its one miss is a language label). On the same subset: sarvam-105b 93%, Qwen3-30B thinking 97%, Sarvam-30B 67% without thinking. Every cloud model in the price-matched tier beats both self-hosted options. Because this set saturates at the top, the frontier runs add little.
  • Sarvam-30B reads the Indic text fine; it loses on following output instructions. It gets order id 100%, amount 100%, intent 100% and invoice fields 97%. But only 23% of its CRM notes are in English with the date as YYYY-MM-DD: it often writes the note in the customer's language (30% non-English without thinking, 80% with thinking) and keeps dates as '13 ऑगस्ट 2026'. It labels the ticket language correctly 20% of the time, calling Tamil, Telugu and Bengali tickets 'hinglish' or 'english'. Qwen3 makes the same Hindi/Marathi/Hinglish confusions but gets the other scripts right (67%).
  • Thinking does not help Sarvam-30B here: 61% vs 63%. It averages 1,610 output tokens per item (vs 66) and p50 latency rises from 8.6 s to 150 s on the shared GPU. Qwen3 gains 7 points from thinking at 386 tokens per item.
  • sarvam-105b is better with reasoning OFF (94%) than ON (80%). With reasoning on, 15 of 90 JSON answers break. 7 have keys and values translated into the customer's language, e.g. {"सेंटिमेंट": "पॉजिटिव", "एस्केलेट": फॉल्स}, and 8 do not parse. 23% of CRM notes also come out non-English. Reasoning on also costs 11x more at list price (₹9.43 vs ₹0.87 for 150 items; 143k reasoning tokens) and is 7x slower (p50 4.6 s vs 0.6 s).
  • Speed on dedicated measurement servers, thinking off, same business prompt. Sarvam-30B Q4_K_M on GPU: prompt 1,003-1,031 tok/s, generation 26.4-27.4 tok/s single-stream, TTFT 1.07 s, aggregate 40-56 tok/s with 4 concurrent requests. Qwen3-30B-A3B Q4_K_M: 776-787 tok/s, 18.5-18.7 tok/s, TTFT 3.2-3.6 s, aggregate 26-28 tok/s. The same prompt is 1,014 Sarvam tokens vs 2,428 Qwen3 tokens (the token tax, see uc12), so Sarvam reaches its first token about 3x sooner.
  • Memory on GPU: peak RSS 20.6 GB (Sarvam) and 24-25 GB (Qwen3); RSS includes the memory-mapped weights, and phys_footprint is 1.1 GB and 5.4-5.6 GB. CPU-only server: RSS 35.5 / 40.5 GB, footprint 19 / 21 GB, because the weights are repacked into anonymous memory. A 32 GB box is too small for CPU-only serving of either model; 48-64 GB is the floor.
  • CPU-only (llama.cpp -ngl 0 -dev none, 6 threads) emulating a GPU-less office box. Sarvam-30B: 12.4 tok/s prompt, 3.0 tok/s generation, 92 s to first token on a 1,014-token prompt. Qwen3-30B-A3B: 11.2 / 2.4 tok/s, 352 s on its 2,428-token version. With 4 concurrent users throughput collapses (0.8 / 0.3 tok/s aggregate). This was measured under heavy load from other jobs (see caveats), but even so it is a batch-processing setup, not a chat setup.
  • By language (fully correct, no thinking), Sarvam-30B vs Qwen3: Hindi 76% vs 92%, Marathi 64% vs 80%, Tamil 56% vs 88%, Telugu 56% vs 92%, Bengali 56% vs 92%, Hinglish 68% vs 60%. Hinglish is the only language where Sarvam-30B leads.
  • Quirks found. (a) The official Sarvam-30B GGUF ignores enable_thinking=false: the template adds <|nothink|> but the model still reasons for ~1k tokens. Only prefilling an empty '<think></think>' assistant turn turns thinking off, and common.bench.chat() has no way to do that, so its sarvam-30b-local always thinks. (b) The Sarvam API returned 402 'No credits available' for about 2 hours mid-run (192 calls; retried later, not scored), then 429 rate-limit errors that outlasted bench.py's 6 retries. (c) gemini-3.8-flash ignores thinking_budget=0: 105 of 150 'thinking off' calls still reported thought tokens (34k total, max 804 per call).

Caveats

  • Synthetic, hand-written data. The author is not a native speaker of all six languages and the items have not been native-reviewed. There are 5 scenarios per task repeated across 6 languages, so 25 distinct scenarios; per-task CIs are about ±10-15 points.
  • gemini-3.8-flash scores 100%, so the set has a ceiling and cannot separate the top systems. It separates the self-hosted options well.
  • The format checks (English note, YYYY-MM-DD date, language labels, digits) measure instruction-following, which is what downstream code needs. A human might accept '13 ऑगस्ट 2026'. Fact-only checks (crm_order_id, crm_amount, triage_intent_urgency, extract_*) are reported separately.
  • Hindi and Marathi tickets contain English loanwords (UPI, OTP, GST). Some systems call them 'hinglish', which is scored as wrong.
  • Sarvam-30B was tested only as the official Q4_K_M GGUF, the only quantisation Sarvam ships. A Q8 or BF16 build may score higher.
  • All speed numbers come from a shared Mac with load averages of 15-560 during the runs. Other suites were hitting the same GPU. Absolute tok/s are pessimistic; the Sarvam vs Qwen3 comparison was measured back-to-back, twice for GPU. Per-item latencies in 'speed' for local systems include queueing behind other suites; use 'hardware' for throughput.
  • The 'aggregate_gen_tok_per_s' figure at concurrency 4 is generated tokens divided by batch wall time, which includes prompt processing.
  • Frontier systems (gemini-pro-latest, gpt-5.5, claude-sonnet-5.5) ran only on SUBSET: per task, the item whose (scenario - language index) mod 5 == 0, one per language, 30 items. Compare them using overall_all_correct_subset30, not overall_all_correct. That metric still has a ±10-15 point CI.

Use case 11Sarvam behind

Bharat Code: coding agents for Indian business logic, prompted in Indian languages

Can these models act as coding agents for Indian business logic when the developer writes the task in their own language (Hindi, Tamil, Hinglish) instead of English? And can they drive a payments-app tool schema from Indian-language voice commands?

uc11 Bharat Code (40 tasks x 4 prompt languages) + 50 tool-calling commands · n=160 · synthetic, written for this benchmark · licence: CC-BY-4.0 (authored here)

Verdict

For an Indian team building fintech, GST or HR logic with an AI coding assistant, any of the price-matched cloud models works. Gemini-3.8-flash (100% first try, think off), Claude Haiku 5.5 (99%) and GPT-5.4-mini with thinking (98%) all reach 97-100% after test-feedback repair, in English, Hindi, Tamil and Hinglish alike. Frontier models are not needed for this class of task. Sarvam-105b is not yet a reliable coding agent for this work. Use it only with thinking on and a test loop (83% within 3 attempts, ~46 s and ~8.5k tokens per solved task), retry its frequent empty replies, and never trust it with checksum algorithms (Verhoeff/Aadhaar) without tests. For Indian-language voice-command tool calling, Sarvam-105b, Gemini, Claude and GPT score 94-100% on these payment commands (thinking-on variants 98-100%; the misses are fractional amounts like paune teen sau = 275), so choose on price, latency or data residency. Watch OpenAI's Responses-API strict default with optional arguments. If you must self-host, Qwen3-30B-A3B beat the official Sarvam-30B Q4 GGUF on code (42% vs 20%) and on tool calls, and was about 10x faster. Neither is usable as an unattended coding agent.

Findings

  • Gemini-3.8-flash (think off) solved every task in every language on the first try: pass@1 100% (95% CI 100%-100%, n=160). Sarvam-105b reached 56% (95% CI 48%-63%, n=160) with thinking off and 68% (95% CI 61%-75%, n=160) with thinking on (temperature 0.5, as Sarvam's docs recommend for thinking mode).
  • Test-feedback repair helps Sarvam: thinking on goes from 68% to 83% within 3 attempts, and thinking off goes from 56% to 64%. With thinking off at temperature 0, Sarvam-105b re-sent byte-identical code in 63 of 131 repair turns (48%), even though the failing asserts were in its context. At temperature 0.7 that drops to 18%, and pass@3 is 67% vs 64%, but pass@1 falls to 51%.
  • Sarvam-105b thinking mode often never answers. In 71 of 245 calls (29%) it used the whole 16k-token budget on reasoning and returned content=null. Its reasoning_content was also null, so the tokens are billed and nothing is visible. A 32k-token retry of one such item also ran out. Solved items cost 8539 output tokens and 46.0 s on average, vs 481 tokens and 3.2 s with thinking off (about ₹1.03 vs ₹0.16 per solved item at list price).
  • Ironically, the Aadhaar checksum is Sarvam's blind spot. On the two Verhoeff tasks (validate an Aadhaar-format number, generate a check digit), Sarvam-105b solved 0% of 8 items first try with thinking off and 0% with thinking on, vs Gemini-3.8-flash 100%. Its Verhoeff implementations either crashed (IndexError/TypeError on the tables) or returned wrong check digits. Other consistent Sarvam failures were compact '1.25 Cr' formatting, advance-tax instalment boundaries (on 15 Sep it returned 15% instead of 45%), and GST invoices where it rounded the total tax and then floor-halved it (898 paise) instead of computing CGST and SGST separately as specified (899).
  • Language penalty (English pass@1 minus the other language, paired by task): Sarvam-105b with thinking off loses +0.17 on Hinglish (CI +0.00 to +0.35), +0.12 on Hindi and +0.07 on Tamil. With thinking on the penalty disappears (hi -0.05, ta -0.03, hinglish -0.05; all CIs span 0). Gemini scores 100% in every language, so it has no measurable penalty. Writing the task in Tamil or Hindi did not hurt any system by a statistically clear margin. The only borderline case is Sarvam with thinking off on Hinglish and Hindi.
  • Tool calling is solved for this kind of schema. Every API system used native tools (Sarvam /v1/chat/completions accepts OpenAI-style `tools` and `tool_choice`, and returns `tool_calls`). sarvam-105b: base 100%, hard 100%; sarvam-105b-think: base 100%, hard 95%; gemini-3.8-flash: base 100%, hard 100%; gemini-3.8-flash-think: base 100%, hard 100%; gpt-5.4-mini: base 97%, hard 95%; gpt-5.4-mini-think: base 100%, hard 100%; claude-haiku-5.5: base 97%, hard 90%; claude-haiku-5.5-think: base 100%, hard 100%; gemini-pro-latest-think: base 100%, hard 100%; gpt-5.5-think: base 100%, hard 100%; claude-sonnet-5.5-think: base 100%, hard 100%; sarvam-30b-local: base 73%, hard 40%; qwen3-30b-local: base 90%, hard 80%. Hard items include 'पौने दो हज़ार' (1750), 'paune teen sau' (275), 'সাড়ে তিনশো' (350), 'ஈபி பில்' (electricity) and 'Tata Play' (DTH).
  • Price-matched cloud tier (full set, n=160): gpt-5.4-mini pass@1 92% (88%-96%), pass@3 98%; gpt-5.4-mini-think pass@1 98% (95%-99%), pass@3 100%; claude-haiku-5.5 pass@1 99% (98%-100%), pass@3 100%; claude-haiku-5.5-think pass@1 99% (98%-100%), pass@3 100%. So Sarvam-105b trails all three price-matched competitors by 30 points or more on first try. Its gap persists after repair (83% vs 100%-100%).
  • Frontier tier (thinking on; task ids 1-30 plus odd ids 31-39, x 4 languages, n=140): gemini-pro-latest-think pass@1 99%, pass@3 100%; gpt-5.5-think pass@1 98%, pass@3 100%; claude-sonnet-5.5-think pass@1 96%, pass@3 100%. On the same subset gemini-3.8-flash scores 100% and sarvam-105b-think 69%. Frontier models add nothing over the cheap tier here, because the suite saturates.
  • No non-Sarvam cloud model shows a language penalty above +0.07 in any language (English minus Hindi/Tamil/Hinglish pass@1). For these models, writing the task in your own language is free.
  • OpenAI quirks: /v1/chat/completions rejects function tools combined with reasoning_effort for gpt-5.4-mini ("use /v1/responses"), so OpenAI thinking-mode tool calls use the Responses API. On /v1/responses, function tools default to strict=true, which makes every property required. The models then filled optional args with mobile="" and amount=0 (which would pay ₹0), dropping exact-match to 74% for both gpt-5.4-mini-think and gpt-5.5-think. With strict=false the reported numbers apply; the strict run is kept in data/uc11_bharat_code/tools_openai_responses_strict.jsonl.
  • Gemini thinking on did slightly worse than off: pass@1 94% vs 100%. 9 of its 9 first-try misses were runaway thinking that hit the 16k cap before the code was finished. This run used temperature 0, and Google recommends 1.0 for Gemini 3.
  • sarvam-30b-local (self-hosted Q4_K_M, single shot, 20-task subset x 4 languages, n=80): pass@1 20%. On the same subset, sarvam-105b scores 61% and gemini-3.8-flash 100%. Sarvam-30B needs an empty <think></think> prefill to stop it reasoning for 4000+ tokens on a 3-line task. Even without thinking, 100% of its answers ran to the 1500-token cap (repetitive comments, duplicated blocks), and median latency was 122 s on the shared Mac.
  • qwen3-30b-local (self-hosted Q4_K_M, single shot, 20-task subset x 4 languages, n=80): pass@1 42%. On the same subset, sarvam-105b scores 61% and gemini-3.8-flash 100%. Median latency was 10 s on the shared Mac.
  • sarvam-30b-local tool calling (llama-server --jinja, native tools): exact 60% (95% CI 46%-74%, n=50); base 73%, hard 40%. It got 1 of 7 fractional-amount commands right (e.g. 'पौने दो हज़ार' -> 900), and in 7 commands it sent amount=0 for 'pay the full bill' instead of omitting the argument, which would pay ₹0.
  • qwen3-30b-local tool calling (llama-server --jinja, native tools): exact 86% (95% CI 76%-94%, n=50); base 90%, hard 80%. It got 4 of 7 fractional-amount commands right (e.g. 'पौने दो हज़ार' -> 2500).

Caveats

  • The 40 tasks are well-specified, mostly single-function problems. Gemini-3.8-flash hits the ceiling, so the suite cannot rank models stronger than it, and it cannot measure Gemini's language penalty. Harder multi-file or ambiguous-spec tasks would be needed.
  • Repair mode shows the model the expected values of up to 5 failing asserts, as pytest output would. pass@3 therefore measures convergence with test feedback, not blind correctness. When the reply was empty, the feedback was a NameError because no function was defined.
  • Translations were done by hand for this benchmark (not by any system under test). They were checked by blind Gemini back-translation plus a meaning diff, with 3 ambiguities fixed. No native-speaker review was possible. The Hinglish style is one developer's register.
  • The system prompt is English in every language condition (as in real coding tools). Only the task text and the output instruction are translated.
  • Thinking budgets were capped at 16k output tokens. Sarvam-105b thinking used temperature 0.5 (vendor guidance). A temperature-0 thinking run is kept as the 'sarvam-105b-think-t0' ablation and lands within noise of it. Gemini thinking ran at temperature 0, below Google's recommended 1.0.
  • Local models were run single-shot on a 20-task subset (odd task ids) with a 1500-token cap. The llama-servers were shared with other benchmark suites at ~6-20 tok/s per slot, so their latency figures reflect a loaded machine, not the hardware ceiling.
  • The tool test uses one turn and five tools, and every command has full information. It does not test clarification questions, multi-step plans or refusals.
  • Frontier models ran on task ids 1-30 plus 31, 33, 35, 37, 39 (the brief addendum first-30 subset plus the 20 odd-id local subset; subset20_odd_tasks gives a like-for-like table). OpenAI and Gemini costs are reported as tokens only; OpenRouter's usage.cost is summed as reported.
  • n=40 per language cell: language-penalty CIs are about ±15 points wide. Differences under ~15 points are not resolved.

Code: suites/uc11_bharat_code/ · results: results/uc11_bharat_code.json · every output: results/raw/uc11_bharat_code.jsonl

Use case 12

The Indic token tax

What does each model's tokenizer charge you, in tokens (and so in money, latency and context window), for the same sentence written in each Indian language?

FLEURS transcripts (FLoRes-101 sentences) · n=100 · public data · licence: CC-BY-4.0

Verdict

Claude is the expensive outlier among the cloud models: 1.9-6.6x Sarvam's tokens on Indic text (Kannada and Punjabi worst), and 1.6x even on English. OpenAI's tokenizer sits between Sarvam and Claude (0.8-3.5x Sarvam: cheaper only on Sindhi, worst on Odia). If your traffic is mostly Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Tamil, Urdu or Nepali, Sarvam and Gemini/Gemma tokenize identically, so per-token price is the only cost lever. For Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Gujarati, Punjabi and especially Odia, Sarvam's tokenizer needs 18-60% fewer tokens than Gemini's on the same text. Avoid Qwen3-class byte-level tokenizers for Indic workloads: 3-10x the tokens of English means 3-10x the generation time when self-hosted and a context window that holds 3-10x less Indic text.

Findings

  • Average Indic token tax (tokens vs the same sentence in English, mean over 14 languages): Sarvam (30B/105B tokenizer) 1.55x, Qwen3-30B-A3B 5.89x, Gemma 4 1.89x, Gemini 3.8 Flash (count_tokens) 1.89x, OpenAI gpt-5.4-mini (API prompt_tokens) 2.10x, Claude Haiku 5.5 (OpenRouter prompt_tokens) 3.44x.
  • Sarvam's tokenizer is the cheapest of the 6 on 12/14 Indic languages; per language the cheapest is: Hindi=sarvam, Bengali=sarvam, Marathi=sarvam, Telugu=sarvam, Tamil=sarvam, Gujarati=sarvam, Kannada=sarvam, Malayalam=sarvam, Punjabi=sarvam, Odia=sarvam, Assamese=openai, Urdu=sarvam, Nepali=sarvam, Sindhi=openai.
  • Qwen3 spends this many times more tokens than Sarvam on the same sentence: Odia 7.1x, Telugu 5.0x, Punjabi 4.9x, Kannada 4.7x, Gujarati 4.7x, Malayalam 4.6x, Tamil 4.3x, Bengali 4.3x, Hindi 3.5x, Marathi 3.4x, Nepali 2.9x, Assamese 2.7x, Urdu 2.1x, Sindhi 1.4x (English 1.03x).
  • Worst/best tokenizer spread per language (same sentence): Odia 7.1x, Punjabi 6.6x, Kannada 6.0x, Telugu 5.0x, Gujarati 4.7x, Malayalam 4.6x, Tamil 4.3x, Bengali 4.3x, Hindi 3.5x, Marathi 3.4x, Nepali 2.9x, Assamese 2.8x, Urdu 2.5x, Sindhi 2.3x.
  • Implied sarvam-105b list cost per 1,000 FLEURS sentences sent as input: English INR 0.36, Hindi INR 0.47, Bengali INR 0.45, Marathi INR 0.51, Telugu INR 0.53, Tamil INR 0.53, Gujarati INR 0.55, Kannada INR 0.56, Malayalam INR 0.59, Punjabi INR 0.56, Odia INR 0.51, Assamese INR 0.73, Urdu INR 0.55, Nepali INR 0.56, Sindhi INR 0.74; as generated output (INR 60/1M) multiply by 4.
  • Cross-check: Sarvam API prompt_tokens minus the HF tokenizer count is a constant per sentence (distinct deltas across all 150 sampled sentences: [14]), i.e. the API bills exactly the open tokenizer plus a fixed chat-template overhead.
  • llama.cpp's tokenizer for the official Sarvam-30B GGUF does not exactly match the HF tokenizer on the scripts Sarvam added: sentences (of 10) with a different count - Telugu 4, Gujarati 4, Kannada 5, Malayalam 7, Punjabi 2; deltas range -4 to 4 tokens per sentence; identical for every other language. Minor for cost, but it means the GGUF build sees slightly different token sequences than the model was trained on for Telugu/Gujarati/Kannada/Malayalam/Punjabi.
  • Gemini count_tokens minus Gemma-4 tokenizer count, mean per sentence: English +0.00, Hindi +0.00, Bengali +0.00, Marathi +0.00, Telugu +0.00, Tamil +0.00, Gujarati +0.00, Kannada +0.00, Malayalam +0.00, Punjabi +0.00, Odia +0.00, Assamese +0.00, Urdu +0.00, Nepali +0.00, Sindhi +0.00 (after removing a 1-token request overhead).
  • Sarvam's tokenizer is Gemma's vocabulary with surgery: both have 262,144 entries and 233,116 (89%) are the same token at the same id. 22,843 tokens are new in Sarvam: GURMUKHI 3,561, ORIYA 3,328, KANNADA 2,935, GUJARATI 2,635, TELUGU 2,520, MEETEI 2,333, MALAYALAM 2,067, TIBETAN 1,796, OL 1,320; dropped HANGUL 4,678, LATIN 3,903, THAI 2,142, HIRAGANA 1,969, KATAKANA 1,957, GREEK 1,313, CJK 904, ETHIOPIC 847. That is why Hindi/Bengali/Marathi/Tamil/Urdu/Nepali counts are identical to Gemini's, and Sarvam wins only on the scripts it added.
  • Claude Haiku 5.5 (OpenRouter prompt_tokens) needs this many times Sarvam's tokens for the same sentence: Punjabi 6.6x, Kannada 6.0x, Odia 5.7x, Malayalam 3.8x, Bengali 3.5x, Tamil 3.3x, Telugu 3.0x, Gujarati 2.9x, Marathi 2.7x, Hindi 2.6x, Assamese 2.5x, Urdu 2.5x, Nepali 2.4x, Sindhi 1.9x (English 1.58x).
  • OpenAI gpt-5.4-mini (API prompt_tokens) needs this many times Sarvam's tokens for the same sentence: Odia 3.5x, Punjabi 1.7x, Bengali 1.4x, Tamil 1.4x, Telugu 1.3x, Marathi 1.3x, Kannada 1.3x, Hindi 1.2x, Gujarati 1.2x, Malayalam 1.2x, Urdu 1.1x, Nepali 1.0x, Assamese 1.0x, Sindhi 0.8x (English 1.00x).

Caveats

  • FLEURS sentences are encyclopaedic (Wikipedia-style) prose; chatty business text, code-mixing and numbers may tokenize differently.
  • Gemini prices are not applied (not taken from a verified source); its column is tokens only. The 'tax' multiplier is price-independent and applies to any per-token price.
  • Sindhi FLEURS text is in Arabic (Perso-Arabic) script; Urdu sentences come from ur_pk.
  • Gemini count_tokens adds a fixed per-request overhead, estimated from count_tokens('a') and subtracted.
  • OpenAI and Claude publish no usable tokenizer here (tiktoken is not installed; Claude's is closed), so their counts are API usage.prompt_tokens for the sentence as the only user message, minus a fixed chat overhead estimated as prompt_tokens('a') - 1 (6 tokens for both). If 'a' is not exactly one token the error is a constant +-1 per sentence. 4 Claude sentences tripped OpenRouter's content filter (no usage returned) and were counted inside a 'Translate this sentence to English:' frame with the frame's tokens subtracted.
  • Tokens per sentence is only half the cost story: a model that needs fewer tokens but answers worse is not cheaper.

Code: suites/uc12_token_tax/ · results: results/uc12_token_tax.json · every output: results/raw/uc12_token_tax.jsonl

For developers

API quirks we hit

  • Sarvam-30B returns "deprecated" on the API; only sarvam-105b and sarvam-105b-conversations remain.
  • Sarvam-105B: reasoning_effort: "low" still spent about 1,300 reasoning tokens on a one-line task; null turns thinking off.
  • Sarvam-105B thinking can return content: null after spending the whole budget, with no visible reasoning either.
  • Out of credits: chat returns HTTP 402 insufficient_quota_error; Sarvam Vision's /start returns HTTP 400 "Insufficient credits", so a 402-only check misses it.
  • Sarvam Vision accepts only PDF or ZIP uploads (wrap an image in a one-file ZIP) and returns a ZIP with markdown whose tables are HTML.
  • Saaras batch names output files 0.json, 1.json… by upload order, so two jobs downloaded into one folder overwrite each other. Map outputs through the job status instead.
  • The Saaras batch endpoint is documented two ways; /speech-to-text/job/v1 with a job_parameters body works.
  • Saaras codemix mode returned no Latin letters at all in 30% of outputs, and wrote numbers as words ("बारह हज़ार").
  • Saaras writes Sindhi in Devanagari only; FLEURS and most Sindhi users expect Perso-Arabic script.
  • Bulbul's REST response holds audio in an audios list; its streaming endpoint delivered complete audio about 3× faster than REST.
  • Odia's language code is od-IN. Mayura accepts at most 1,000 characters per request.
  • Sarvam's chat endpoint accepts OpenAI-style tools and returns tool_calls.
  • Sarvam API prompt_tokens equals the open tokenizer's count plus 14 tokens per request.
  • Sarvam-30B GGUF ignores enable_thinking: false, reasoning_effort and <|nothink|>; prefill an empty <think></think> via /completion.
  • Gemini 3.8 Flash refused 3–6% of harmless audio clips with BlockedReason.OTHER, and still reported thought tokens on most calls with thinking_budget: 0.
  • gemini-embedding-2 does not support task_type, and a list of strings in one request returns one merged embedding.
  • Gemini Pro and Claude Sonnet 5.5 cannot turn thinking off.
  • Gemini TTS multi-speaker needs speech_metadata.speaker on every text part; a plain "Doctor: …" script returns HTTP 400.
  • OpenAI whisper-1 rejects bn, ml, te, gu and pa as language hints; gpt-4o-transcribe rejects pa and or.
  • Through OpenRouter, Claude's content filter blocked four ordinary news sentences (one about Ebola) with no token usage returned.
  • A Gemini Python client call can hang indefinitely without an explicit HttpOptions(timeout=…).
  • OpenAI rejects function tools combined with reasoning_effort on /v1/chat/completions for GPT-5.4 mini; use /v1/responses.
  • On /v1/responses, function tools default to strict: true, making every argument required: GPT models then sent amount: 0 for "pay the full bill" (74% exact). With strict: false they scored 100%.

Cost

What the benchmark cost to run

About ₹1,200 of Sarvam credit at list prices (₹1,500 topped up), a few US dollars of OpenAI usage (recorded as tokens), US$3.75 on OpenRouter for Claude, and a few million Gemini tokens. Sarvam's translation APIs were the single biggest line: about ₹300 for 150,000 characters of legal text, which Sarvam-105B translated just as faithfully for about ₹2. List prices used: speech-to-text ₹30 per audio hour (₹45 with speaker labels), Sarvam-105B ₹15 / ₹60 per million input / output tokens, Bulbul ₹30 per 10,000 characters, Sarvam Vision ₹0.50 per page, translation about ₹20 per 10,000 characters.

Reproduce

Run it yourself

git clone https://github.com/shivanathd/sarvam-field-test
cd sarvam-field-test
cp .env.example .env        # SARVAM_API_KEY, GOOGLE_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY
python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
scripts/serve_local.sh      # optional: self-hosted Sarvam-30B and Qwen3-30B via llama.cpp
.venv/bin/python suites/uc08_quick_commerce/run.py api   # any suite; reruns skip finished items
.venv/bin/python report/build_report.py                  # rebuild this page from results/

Everything is open source at github.com/shivanathd/sarvam-field-test: every script, test set, result and raw model output, so the report rebuilds without any API key.
